#6741. Why Do We Keep Coming Back to Godzilla?

Like most people born in the western world after 1954, I knew of a monster named Godzilla before I’d heard of a country called Japan. It’s not a rare perspective. For as long as nearly any living person can remember, Godzilla has been hugely popular, far exceeding the global recognition afforded most leaders, athletes, and certainly his human co-stars, those men and women whose dramatic dealings are the universally agreed-upon bargain for apocalyptic havoc that millions upon millions have gladly paid to see for over 70 years.

What Godzilla hasn’t been is prestigious. The irradiated dinosaur of very few words—mainly deafening screams—is a beloved figure more in the key of Harry Potter, Batman, or James Bond than the loftier fare that typically gets recognized by major festivals or awards bodies. But exceptions to the rule do exist. The Criterion Collection issued Ishiro Honda's 1954 original on a deluxe Blu-ray in 2012 and marked their 1,000th release with a lavish set of Godzilla’s Shōwa era (1954-1975), which both documents film history and calls to mind John Huston’s Chinatown line about sticking around long enough to become respectable. Writing an introduction to Honda’s biography A Life in Film, from Godzilla to Kurosawa, Martin Scorsese deemed the series’ first director "an extraordinary artist and craftsman" and placed Honda’s 1954 film (alongside spin-offs Mothra and Rodan) among “pictures that haunted the imaginations of young moviegoers like myself and millions of others for years to come.” Kiyoshi Kurosawa—perhaps Japan’s greatest living filmmaker, and certainly its finest practitioner of austere horror—deemed Honda’s film an early lesson in national trauma. Thomas Pynchon, too, had ambitious plans to write a novel about the insurance adjuster who responds to Godzilla’s wreckage (the idea never fully materialized, though it did become a nice tangent in his 1990 novel Vineland). We can look at the films and countenance such appreciations from geniuses. In the meantime, good luck to anyone counting the exact number of action figures, coloring books, sticker packs, and lunchboxes boasting Godzilla and friends.

A critical shift started somewhere in the last decade. Toho ostensibly shelved Godzilla with 2004’s Final Wars, a grand finale that was the big-budget equivalent of a child smashing toys. (That is a compliment.) Godzilla LLC boasts enough films and ancillary products to be financially solvent until the sun burns out (or an indomitable monster rises from the sea), but that retirement was short-lived. Toho resurrected the franchise in aggressive form with 2016’s Shin Godzilla, both a complete series reboot and (across several stages, each grotesque and terrifying) character reinvention that dispensed with typical monster-movie hijinks. An unholy experiment that would make the series’ many mad scientists proud, Shin Godzilla fused the hilarious bureaucratic hallway-rushing of In the Loop or Veep with cosmic horror befitting its director, Hideaki Anno, whose contributions to Japanese culture are nearly Godzilla’s equal on the strength of Neon Genesis Evangelion alone. With time, it’s downright eerie to see Anno’s foreshadowing of the global unrest of Trump, Brexit, COVID, and our endless misinformation era. But rather than keep the great filmmaker on retainer for any number of sequels or spin-offs, Toho regrettably followed Shin Godzilla with an anime trilogy produced for Netflix, a rare class of films I’ve been too embarrassed to even log on Letterboxd.

Whether genius or dreck, none of these films quite anticipated 2023’s Godzilla Minus One. It’s one thing to become the highest-grossing Japanese-language release in U.S. history—any Godzilla movie that doesn't at least aim for such a distinction isn’t worth its salt. It’s harder to imagine anyone, even or especially the franchise’s most ardent fans, anticipated lavish public praise from a quintet of Best Director winners in Steven Spielberg (who claims to have seen the film at least three times), James Cameron (who offered to work on a sequel), Christopher Nolan, Guillermo Del Toro, and Bong Joon-ho. In a recorded conversation with Yamazaki, Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie credited the film as an inspiration; the actor went so far as to call it “perfect.” Which is to say nothing of the fact that Godzilla Minus One earned the series its first Oscar, a VFX prize awarded to none other than writer-director Takashi Yamazaki—a nice encapsulation of the film’s balance between spirit and spectacle.

Because Godzilla Minus One resonated more than anyone could have anticipated, Godzilla Minus Zero, which arrives in theaters this weekend, shoulders the burden of expectation. The first shot across the bow was its world premiere at last month’s New York Film Festival, where Zero debuted alongside prestige fare like Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial and Tony Gilroy’s star-studded Behemoth! There, NYFF’s artistic director Dennis Lim introduced the movie to a sold-out crowd at the Alice Tully Hall, praising Yamazaki for exemplifying "the endless possibilities of creative VFX and genre filmmaking." Minus Zero indeed thrives on spectacle: its opening sequence blazes a merciless path of carnage aided by an elegant long take, while subsequent scenes centered on one of Godzilla’s classic foes, the three-headed Ghidorah, inspire genuine terror more than cheap thrills. This is the first Japanese film shot for IMAX, a large-scale exhibition that’s often torqued for discomfort. Yamazaki’s centerpiece battle pitting the monster against a squadron of fighter planes is dogged by fatalistic doom: a mother and child screaming as their house crashes to the ground don’t get the last-minute salvation we’ve come to expect, and even the sentimental-seeming inclusion of a pilot named Honda is complicated by his eventual fate.

If not quite so grave as the visions of death that imprinted upon a young Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Yamazaki’s narrative—including a face-melting sequence that U.S. distributor GKIDS have asked not be spoiled—provides a stark contrast to the bloodless carnage of American blockbusters. It’s quite the cultural coup, too, that a film this brutal and generally skeptical of American imperialism has secured a simultaneous international release: every English-speaking actor (none recognizable, each portraying arrogant allied military) bears an amusingly off-market quality à la the nefarious white time-travelers of 1991’s altogether underrated Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.

Nearly all Godzilla films are a total restart. Minus Zero is immediately notable as a direct sequel. The results suggest that Yamazaki overestimated his initial project. Godzilla is not much of a presence in Minus Zero, first appearing around the 50-minute mark and then again in a suitable, albeit brief climax. Far more time is spent with those we came to know and like during Minus One, each reprised by an entirely competent ensemble that fails to elevate interest higher than a certain co-star’s 50 meters. (The protagonists’ adopted daughter from Minus One returns here for the sole purpose of standing in place and crying.) Whatever its pretensions towards grandeur, this is still a film where a scientist explains his master plan by smashing together two monster figures. It takes little to delight in this moment, a literal and figurative collision of serious storytelling and childlike abandon. More of that spirit might’ve served the final picture.

My mild disappointment is nothing compared to the agony Godzilla has wreaked on the district of Ginza, which last week hosted the first public screenings of Minus Zero through the Tokyo International Film Festival. Godzilla’s annihilated the city’s landmarks enough times that when we think of all-out destruction on the sprawling megalopolis that is Tokyo, we’re probably picturing its uber-fashionable shopping sector laid to ruins. When he emerged from the sea in 1954, he wrecked the district’s historic Nichigeki Theater, which was again destroyed (in real life, of humans’ accord) and reopened as the Yurakucho Mullion building in 1984—the same year as The Return of Godzilla, where he inflicted yet more damage on the brand-new structure. Godzilla Minus One recreated the Nichigeki Theater in loving detail only to destroy it again in a sequence that deployed modern visual effects to cause maximum tactility and human misery. That Hiroshima-like site is revisited in Minus Zero, leading one character to declare that “Ginza is again the battleground.” Time’s healed those wounds, however. The night before Minus Zero’s Japanese premiere, a small crowd gathered outside the Yurakucho Mullion’s Seiko watch for an extravagant display: the clock lifted, and out came a small set of Godzilla puppets that strike chimes while Akira Ifukube’s iconic theme plays.

Ginza’s Wako Clock Tower has fared no better: it was torn to ribbons in the 1954 original, 1995’s Godzilla vs. Destoroyah, Shin Godzilla, and Minus One. After a time you must wonder what keeps bringing Godzilla back to the neighborhood. Is it animal instinct, or mere coincidence, or an atomic hatred for its glowing consumerism? The Wako Annex, a nearby pastry shop that Google not-inaccurately describes as “chic,” currently advertises a Christmas-themed cake recreation of the oft-doomed Clock Tower with Minus Zero’s monster looming over it; accompanying text informs us that “Godzilla strikes Ginza’s Wako once again.” The nearby Toho cinema is within Hibiya Godzilla Square, featuring a small but impressively detailed statue and a plaque reading, “The human race must coexist with Godzilla.” Immediately adjacent is a three-story shopping mall hosting a Toho store selling numerous Godzilla ephemera. (I bought the tea cup.)

Even Americans accustomed to the fetishization of disaster would be impressed by Japan’s ability to marry suffering and spectacle to great financial gain. Perhaps it’s the same haunted fascination of a young Martin Scorsese or Kiyoshi Kurosawa cast unto the world at large; Godzilla might be scary as he destroys Ginza, but he’s something to admire when shrunk down to human size and displayed inside the Yurakucho Mullion’s lobby. (The photo-snapping crowds that gather every time I walk past suggest that bit of marketing paid off.) Even as Minus Zero’s first reviews show a less rapturous response than Minus One, this series’ viability—and its newfound prestige—shows little indication of flagging. Ginza’s residents were beyond happy to see Godzilla, at least in ossified, action-figure form. But who's to say they wouldn't be just as excited if, one day, his path of destruction broke through the screen?

#6740. Iowa Governor-Elect Rob Sand Was Also a Prada Model

On November 3, as part of the blue-vote tsunami, Iowa elected Democratic Governor Rob Sand. The 44 year-old graduated with a political science degree from Brown University and a J.D. degree from University of Iowa College of Law; he even got a Truman scholarship and an honors thesis. And his 2026 campaign was centered on anti-corruption, bipartisanship, affordable living, and public education. But there’s more—he’s also a pretty face.

As it turns out, the governor-elect helped pay for his prestigious college degrees by walking runways in Milan and Paris. At six-feet, three inches, the young, aspiring politician modeled in shows for Giuliano Fujiwara and Number (N)ine. He even made it into a Prada runway, Newsweek reports. It was the early 2000s, and he was reportedly signed to none other than IMG Models—though his profile seems to have been taken down since.

For whatever reason, his modeling past is not something the chiseled governor-elect likes to talk about, the New York Times noted, but it sure makes for quite the resume.

On January 19, 2004, Sand even missed the Iowa caucus in Decorah because he was modeling menswear in Milan. “It had to be one or the other,” he told Newsweek. “And I chose to go to Europe.” (Who wouldn’t?) While Sand did not win that time around, look at him now, years later, up at the top.

Sand took Iowa this week while in a sharp navy-blue suit and a sky-blue checkered button-down that matched his eyes. “Thank you, Iowa! I love you, Iowa!” he excitedly said after catwalking up to the podium for his victory speech.

Rob Sand’s team has not responded to Harper’s Bazaar’s request for comment.

#6738. In Brooklyn, an Intimate Diwali Dinner Party Bridging Two Easts

On a Sunday night, the elevator doors open onto Rachel Gurjar’s Brooklyn living room. Amaranthus blooms brush brass family heirlooms and fresh pomegranates on a credenza. A tiffin bearing a relative’s initials rests on draped brown fabric. The room could be a still from Gurjar’s debut cookbook, East to East: Recipes and Stories From Mumbai to New York, released October 13.

Barefoot in a pre-draped blue floral sari, Gurjar moves unhurriedly, labelling plates with scraps of tape. She then pulls a white platter from an immaculately organized glass cabinet. “I think this is for the duck,” she says, already moving on.

Since 2021, Gurjar, who grew up in Mumbai, has thrown New York Diwali parties that have acquired a certain lore. One year, she led magazine editors in choreographed Bollywood dances; another, a pani puri fountain presided over a party for 140, with handmade naan to match. “I didn’t have a place to celebrate Diwali myself, so I decided to throw these parties,” she says.

Tonight, the sixth annual gathering is quieter, and intentionally so: a dozen chefs, artists, and designers who helped bring the book to life, on the page or in spirit. If the official launch party was for the public, this one is for her people.

Diwali, the South Asian festival of lights, is widely associated with the triumph of good over evil. It is also an occasion to gather, feed one another, and take stock. Gurjar’s chosen family spans disciplines, with an emphasis on the Black, Brown, and AAPI creatives whose work, she believes, makes New York what it is. “I wanted to make sure that every person at the table had a medium through which they expressed their creativity,” she explains.

Guests include collaborators like designer Ivan Lam of Tender Touch Studios, who picked up flowers that morning; food stylist Sean Dooley, who styled the book’s visuals; and photographer Isa Zapata, a former Bon Appétit colleague who photographed it in Mumbai.

The evening begins with an actually spicy pani puri mezcalita and masala popcorn. Whipped masala and curry leaf butters sit in vintage coupes beside a sweet-sour pomegranate Chex Mix that took Gurjar 12 attempts to perfect. Bollywood music plays as guests pass around bindis and apply them to one another.

The menu moves between Mumbai and New York, yet feels unmistakably familial. Gurjar’s mother, Ranjana, brought potato and rice chips she made in India, sneaking them past TSA. She also spent the week helping her daughter prepare, kneading dough and frying gulab jamun.

“At her core, Rachel is a nurturer,” says chef Josh Osamor, who calls her goat curry one of the most delicious things he has eaten. The two recently collaborated on a Nigerian-Indian supper club. “The biryani jollof was a no-brainer. It was a perfect dance,” he says.

Leanne Gan, an art director at the ACLU, has attended Gurjar’s Diwali parties since the beginning. Adjusting her sea-green dupatta, she dips a rice chip into the Penang curry crab dip. “Rachel is someone who doesn’t settle for less,” Gan says. “It’s been amazing to see her put 110% of herself into these recipes.”

The room erupts with oohs and aahs as artist and fashion designer Misha Japanwala arrives in a gold-and-silver lamé sari and a custom silver breastplate she made using body casting, the same process she used for pieces for Cardi B and Lizzo. (Most recently, Lupita Nyong’o wore Japanwala’s work in The Odyssey.)

“I just felt like I was missing a silver breastplate in my wardrobe, and everybody needs a silver breastplate,” she jokes. She accessorizes with nipple-cast rings and silver jewelry from Karachi, her hometown.

“One of the most beautiful things about moving to New York has been expanding my South Asian circle and being able to celebrate each other in this way,” Japanwala reflects. When she hosted Eid at home for the first time last year, she invited friends from her wider South Asian circle, beyond Muslim Pakistanis. “It really was the most miraculous thing,” she adds. Next to her, fashion designer Sheena Sood of Abacaxi is wearing a mirrorwork lehenga with a matching knit shrug from a 2021 collection.

The contagious joys of Diwali extend beyond the subcontinent: For Manouska Jeantus, founder of the social events company Nous Love Club, the gathering recalls celebrating Haitian Independence Day with her family, even as she eats malai shrimp instead of the soup joumou she grew up with.

Guests take their seats, and Gurjar raises a dirty chai espresso martini for a quick toast. Dinner is a greatest-hits collection from East to East, starting with achari melon salad with tempered pickling spices and garam masala roasted squash slicked with brown butter and lime. Back in the kitchen, Gurjar works two cast-iron skillets at once, searing scored duck breasts for her paanch phoran duck—a crowd favorite—and finishing them with raspberry chimichurri. Platters of rice arrive with naan she and her mother made that morning.

Dessert brings homemade gulab jamun and cardamom sticky toffee cake, which Gurjar floods with caramel and finishes with flaky salt. Osamor shakes up another round of dirty chai espresso martinis. A little dancing gives way to conversation on the couch about the week ahead. It is, after all, a school night, and everyone is pleasantly overfed.

The meal mirrors the book’s central idea: a refusal to draw a neat line between East and West. East to East also makes room for what a cooking reel can leave out: the distance from home, building a career abroad, and watching parents grow older from afar, and other complexities that extend beyond homesickness.

In a rare chapter titled “Cultural Appropriation: Who Really Pays,” Gurjar asks who really benefits when food travels, and who gets left behind. It’s a question she and her creative peers have long discussed. To her, celebrating food’s ability to connect people also means asking who gets to tell its stories.

When I first met Gurjar two years ago at a party, I told her she’d taught me to make perfect short ribs, her Thai-inflected coconut braise. What I didn’t tell her was how rare it felt to see another Indian immigrant pursue a creative path, or how brave I thought she was. She has become that person for others, too, inspiring adventurous cooking and a willingness to take up space.

Some had made a career like hers seem out of reach. “I had experiences where people made me feel it wasn’t an option for me,” Gurjar laments. “Brown people, we’re often scared to dream big because we’ve never been permitted to. And I’m in a phase of life when I’m not saying no to anything.”

Asked about the highlight of her career, Gurjar doesn’t have to look backward. She sips her chai espresso martini and says, “I think I’m living it right now.”

#6737. Erika Felt the “Math Wasn’t Really Mathing” With Blake’s Finances During ‘Love Is Blind’

There was a lot more to their breakup than we saw.

Erika and Blake were one of the many (many!) couples to end Love Is Blind Season 11 without getting married, and apparently there was more to their split than we saw on screen.

The show’s finale gave viewers a brief glimpse at Erika and Blake ending their relationship seemingly due to logistical issues: he wanted to live on a boat and sail around the world, while she wanted to live in a house and start a family. But Erika says there were some other red flags.

“I was like, ‘There’s no way this guy’s broke.’ He’s got a career and not a lot of bills from what I heard. So the math wasn’t really mathing,” she told Tudum. “Those are questions that maybe I was too afraid to ask at the beginning. They’re very sensitive and personal. But I remember him being so cool about [finances] that it almost felt like he did have money in the moment. He wasn’t sweating about it at all.”

She added that “Finances are something that, over time, you start to see some patterns and traits. Like, ‘What credit cards are they using? Are they paying with cash?’”

On top of that, Erika felt like she hadn’t really gotten to experience Blake’s world and didn’t know what she was jumping into. She literally thought to herself, “‘I can’t marry you, I haven’t seen enough of your life,’” adding, “It just started to feel really dangerous to get any closer to the wedding having already been through a divorce.”

#6736. 35 Gifts for Boyfriends Who've Been Very Good This Year 2026

The internet has some peculiar ideas about what constitutes a good gift for a boyfriend. Search long enough and you'll find yourself in a purgatory of ergonomic footrests, rechargeable headlamps, novelty T-shirts, and footwear that seem designed to extinguish whatever romantic spark remains. Surely the person you love deserves something a little more inspired.

The first step in closing the swag gap is a first-rate white tee. Merz b. Schwanen makes them in all manner of cuts and styles, but the 215, famously worn by Jeremy Allen White in The Bear, hits the sweet spot.

Tekla and Auralee are back for their second collaboration, and these checked pajama pants sit right in the middle of the Venn diagram of cozy and covetable. Definitely a pair he should wear out of the house.

Handsewn in Maine, Easymoc’s Cozymoc pairs a full-grain leather upper with a 100% shearling lining for shuffling around in comfort. A Vibram sole makes it fit for trips outside, and it’s resoleable, too.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The whole point of a gift set is to give him something he wouldn’t try himself. Fortunately for you, after using this Mojave Ghost body wash, lotion, and hand cream, he’s never going to want to go back to whatever he was using before.

DedCool’s cult-favorite Xtra Milk scent gets the body scrub treatment, which means he can exfoliate his way to softer skin while smelling like the best version of himself.

#6734. The Best Korean Exfoliator to Get (and Maintain) Glass Skin

If there’s one common denominator among Korean skin-care products, be they cleansers or toners, it’s that they prioritize the skin barrier. With this context, the best Korean exfoliators may seem a little counterintuitive—after all, face exfoliants can sometimes do more harm than good, relying on strong active ingredients (or high concentrations) and inadvertently leaving skin dry or irritated.

But that’s the beauty of the Korean approach to resurfacing skin. “K-beauty favors gentle, more frequent exfoliation that protects the skin barrier,” says Jane Yoo, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York, NY. “To this effect, K-beauty utilizes low-concentration acids, enzyme powders, or peeling gels that roll dead skin off the surface.” These light-handed exfoliating formulas also considered a critical part of a daily routine aimed towards getting (and maintaining) glass skin—and a natural counterpart to moisturizing. “Exfoliating is usually followed by layers of hydration to support the barrier as the goal is the same: achieve smooth skin but with less irritation,” says Dr. Yoo. With that in mind, consider these worth adding to your regimen.

Exfoliation works on multiple levels to refine and resurface skin—making it one of the most impactful steps in any skin-care routine. At its most basic, “exfoliation helps to remove the outermost layer of dead skin cells in the stratum corneum, promoting skin cell turnover and revealing brighter, smoother and more even-toned skin,” says Dr. Chang.

It can also clear debris from pores, which helps reduce whiteheads, blackheads, and other forms of acne. And in helping shed those dead skin cells that would otherwise pile up on skin’s surface, “exfoliation can also help improve the absorption of active ingredients like vitamin C or retinoids,” she says.

Unlike Western exfoliation habits—which tend to be more aggressive—“Korean skin-care routines emphasize the regular use of gentler topicals to achieve radiant skin without irritation,” says Dr. Chang. One big point of difference is that in the U.S., many formulations tend to focus on correcting issues, be they acne, dullness, or dark spots.

However, Koreans prioritize prevention and consistency. As a result, “you’ll rarely find harsh scrubs or aggressive peels,” says Cho. “The majority of K-beauty exfoliants use mild chemical exfoliants such as PHA, because they clear dead skin cells without irritation.” Fermented enzymes and natural fruit extracts are also popular, since they tend to be well tolerated even by those with sensitive skin, according to Dr. Chang.

How often you exfoliate ultimately depends on your skin type and the sort of exfoliant you’re using. For example, if you have dry or sensitive skin, exfoliating once or twice a week with a mild acid may suffice, says Dr. Chang. Meanwhile, “for those with oily or acne-prone skin, people may tolerate light daily exfoliation with ingredients like salicylic acid,” she says.

Ultimately, the strength of your exfoliant plays a large role. “Higher strength exfoliants should be used less frequently, while very gentle exfoliators could be used daily in those who tolerate it well,” says Dr. Chang. If you’re using a Korean exfoliant, then it’s likely gentle enough to use daily or every other day (but again, that depends). Ultimately, she says, “the key is to monitor for signs of over-exfoliation—like stinging, redness, flaking, or tightness—and adjust the frequency accordingly.”

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to the best Korean exfoliator, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, exfoliant type, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

#6732. Montana’s Newest Congressman Dresses Like a Ralph Lauren Model

You couldn’t ask for a better embodiment of the blue wave than Sam Forstag, the 32-year-old rookie Montana Democrat who defeated his Republican rival in yesterday’s midterms to flip an important House seat. While unaffordability was a key issue in the midterms across the country, it’s especially noticeable in Montana, where an influx of billionaires and tech companies has sent the cost of living soaring. Like many of his compatriots, Forstag campaigned on promises of affordable housing, better healthcare, and getting money out of politics. Unlike his fellow Democratic challengers, however, he did it in a wardrobe that looked straight off a rack at the RRL store.

Last night, in front of a crowd of supporters in Missoula, Forstag delivered his victory speech dressed in a hickory-striped work shirt, jeans, a big western belt buckle, and a pair of weathered brown forestry boots. Forstag’s fit stands in contrast to the standard election night business-casual look favored by political hopefuls on both sides of the aisle, but he’s far from the first candidate to lean into the dress codes of blue-collar Americans. From Tim Walz’s camo hats and Filson Mackinaw jackets to John Fetterman’s Carhartt hoodie, workwear remains a potent symbol of working-class solidarity. In this case, however, it’s not just blue-collar cosplay.

Forstag at a student get-out-the-vote gathering at Montana State University in October.

Straight out of college and looking to pay off his student loans, Forstag joined the US Forest Service as a wildland firefighter and spent the next eight years battling blazes around the country, including four years as a smokejumper parachuting into fire zones. As a result, he comes by his love of Levi’s and sturdy, Goodyear-welted footwear honestly, and—Montana being a place where jeans and work shirts are considered business-casual for many—didn’t need to change his look for the campaign.

Forstag addressing voters at a town hall in August.

As authentic as Forstag’s election-night outfit was, he also appears to be a guy who understands the power of styling. While his shirt likely didn’t have Ralph Lauren’s initials on the tag (wildland firefighters only make $20 an hour), the way he wore it—half unbuttoned, layered over a red thermal henley, and tucked into his jeans—owes a debt to the romantic take on Western style Lauren has been trafficking in since the ’70s. Or, equally likely, the Montana cowboys who the designer borrowed it from. Either way, Forstag’s look, like the progressive politics he and his Democratic colleagues campaigned on, will be a welcome disruption to business as usual on Capitol Hill.

#6731. Carolyn Murphy Steps Into La DoubleJ’s Kaleidoscopic World With a Joyful Collection

The “Sisterhood of Light” capsule turns classic La DoubleJ silhouettes into festive showstoppers.

There was a little kismet in Carolyn Murphy and J.J. Martin finding each other. When they met, Murphy had recently lost her home in the Palisades to the devastating California wildfires, not far from where Martin grew up. That encounter brought them together as friends and now as collaborators, as the pair teamed on a holiday capsule collection, “Sisterhood of Light.”

“She was the dose of joy that I needed,” the model tells ELLE of Martin. “We love a little woo-woo here, a little woo-woo there. But also what I love about J.J. is how grounded she is at the same time. And she’s obviously got great taste.”

While Murphy and Martin instantly hit it off, La DoubleJ’s maximalist, kaleidoscopic world is a departure from Murphy’s own more pared-back style. “I’m kind of a minimalist,” Murphy remembers telling Martin. “I don’t really wear pattern and print.” Martin laughed, and the two began exploring how to fuse their worlds.

The capsule interprets La DoubleJ’s signature pieces, most notably its Swing Dress, through Murphy’s lens. The A-line maxi, which celebrates its 10th anniversary this year and was the brand’s first dress silhouette, gets a luminous update in the Super Swing, a showstopper with embroidered dégradé sequins that shift from silver to gold. That luminous sensibility carries over to the Opera Swing, which features a gilded fil coupé jacquard, and the Mini Supreme Swing, a mod-inspired number embroidered with hibiscus blooms.

To bring the collection to life, Murphy modeled the designs at Villa Tarlarini, where photographer Kate Bellm captured the campaign against lush greenery and picturesque seascapes. Murphy looked to Marisa Berenson and Veruschka, whose influence can be seen in her wavy 1970s hair, for the shoot—an inspiration that spoke to her idea of world-building for the holidays and beyond.

“There’s [an] escape and fantasy with it,” she explains. “Even for the Carolyn dress, I was like, ‘Oh, maybe this is Robin Wright Penn in Princess Bride. Oh, maybe this will be a great wedding dress for somebody.’ And buying me a martini dress with this jacket is so cool. To me, that’s Hollywood.”

The capsule gave Murphy a chance not only to step outside her usual style, but also to find a creative outlet as she rebuilt her home and explored what it means to get dressed now. “I’m a fashionista of the early ’90s, and I love anything that’s classic with a twist,” she says. “I had these style icons back then. Carolyn Bessette—who I know has been super popular of late—and Narciso [Rodriguez] were actually friends of mine. They were my earliest definition of, ‘Oh, that’s what I want to look like, and that’s how I want to dress.’”

Now, the model is defining her own style. “After all these years of being dressed by people and being told what to wear, you get to a place in life where you’re like, ‘Well, I’m going to define my own style.’ I just think I’ve always been pretty consistent about that.”

#6728. Coty Sales Decline 2% as Transition Kicks In

For Coty’s first quarter 2027 earnings, the 2% like-for-like sales decline shows an improvement on the last year, when revenues fell 6% and 4% in the first and second halves of fiscal 2026, respectively. The stabilization — sales were at -1% in Q4 2026 — can be credited to growth in key markets like the US, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, as well as fruitful reinvestment in the group’s prestige business that includes Burberry, Hugo Boss and Calvin Klein.

Still, executive chair and interim CEO Markus Strobel was careful to refer to the progress as “green shoots”, which he hopes will translate into positive growth over time. “As we’ve previously shared, 2027 will be a transition year,” he said in a statement released on Wednesday. “We expect the recovery to be uneven, and implementation will take time. We know confidence is earned through consistent delivery, and our goal is to steadily improve execution and translate it into shareholder value in the years ahead.”

Coty.Curated, the French beauty group’s turnaround framework, kicked into motion last fiscal year. A redesign of the organization and cost structure hopes to improve conversion through reinvestment into its portfolio of brands.

The strategy is paying off the most in the prestige segment. Net revenues declined 1% to $1.1 billion in Q1, a contrast to the same quarter a year prior (-4%), and representing 68% of total sales. “We have increasingly concentrated investment behind our top six prestige brands — Burberry, Hugo Boss, Calvin Klein, Marc Jacobs, Chloé, and Kylie Cosmetics — which represented 73% of prestige sales in Q1,” Strobel noted, highlighting the success of new launches including Boss Bottled Beyond for Her, Burberry Goddess Amber Vanilla, Mood Stones by Kylie Jenner, and makeup from Marc Jacobs Beauty.

Earlier this week, Coty announced a 40-year extension of its Marc Jacobs license, which it has held since 2003. The plan is to expand the brand across multiple categories following the successful relaunch of Marc Jacobs Beauty in May. (The beauty offshoot was discontinued in 2021, once its licensing deal with LVMH-owned Kendo ended.)

Strobel said: “The recent launch of Marc Jacobs Beauty makeup is off to a strong start across the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia. The agreement provides Coty with a strong platform to build on that momentum while enhancing the long-term visibility of Coty’s Prestige portfolio.”

The recovery of consumer beauty — including CoverGirl, Rimmel, and Sally Hansen — is slightly slower. While the decline in like-for-like sales narrowed to 3% from 8% in the first half of fiscal 2026, the segment remains negative. Net revenues reached $496.8 million in Q1, declining 3% on a like-for-like basis.

Asia-Pacific led growth across both segments, with sales up 8% to $192 million, driven by higher sales in China, Southeast Asia, and Asia travel retail. Sales were flat across the Americas at $653 million, with particular momentum in Brazil. EMEA (Europe, the Middle East, and Africa) revenues fell 5% to $710 million; the group cited lower sales in the Middle East and Europe.

Coty expects to see a low single-digit decline in Q2, consistent with the last two quarters. As for the full year, the company is still withholding its projection as it gears up to claw back the negative growth seen throughout 2026.

#6727. Abdul El-Sayed Is Winning at Watches, Too

Michigan voters made history Tuesday night by electing Abdul El-Sayed to the US Senate, as part of a greater blue wave that swept the nation. The 44-year-old former epidemiologist is set to become America’s first Muslim senator—and, in a slightly more trivial milestone, might also be the first real-deal watch nerd to reach the Capitol.

During his victory speech, the senator-elect sported a Grand Seiko Spring Drive Chronograph (ref. SBGC249), a limited-edition piece from the Japanese watchmaker that pairs a GMT (which tracks the time across multiple time zones) and a chronograph (i.e. a stopwatch function). Politicians tend to go one of two ways with their timepieces: Either they’ll cosplay as a man of the people with an affordable Timex or Casio, or they’ll sport a luxury watch with historical pedigree—like the Rolex “President” Day-Date, worn by several commanders-in-chief—to make themselves appear ready for higher office. An obscure Grand Seiko fits neither of those categories.

Instead, El-Sayed’s Grand Seiko is a burly sport model made by one of the world’s most elegant watchmakers. At 43.5mm, it’s hefty, a good fit for the senator-elect’s beefed-up forearms. It’s quite complicated, with several different functions, and a dial as busy as Little Caesars Arena during a Detroit Pistons game. It costs $12,400, but you’d have to be very deep into the hobby to recognize its value.

What I find so compelling about El-Sayed’s choice is that it doesn’t appear to be masquerading as some political symbol. It’s simply the excellent wristwear of an honest-to-goodness collector. “Folks who know me know I’m a sucker for automatic watches and sort of classic watches,” El-Sayed said in an interview with LGBT Detroit in May.

Throughout his campaign, he’s worn a wide range of pieces. His recent go-to appears to be a Mühle-Glashütte S.A.R. Rescue-Timer, a great-looking and obscure German tool watch. He also owns the U-1 SE, a large dive watch from the German independent brand Sinn.

Not all of El-Sayed’s timepieces are devoid of political meaning, however. The senator-elect has worn an Omega Speedmaster, the watch worn by American astronauts Buzz Aldrin and Neil Armstrong when they first set foot on the moon. That’s about as patriotic as a watch can get without excerpting the Declaration of Independence on the dial. Naturally, he also owns a Shinola Runwell, from the brand based in El-Sayed’s native Detroit. El-Sayed is very aware of what a certain watch can signal about the wearer. In his 2020 book, Healing Politics: A Doctor’s Journey into the Heart of Our Political Epidemic, he wrote about how seeing Rolex billboards along a highway prompted him to reflect on income inequality: “How many people who drive this road can actually afford one of those?”

But when did I realize that El-Sayed was a true-blue watch guy? It wasn’t the dialed-in collection of interesting tool watches that did it, but his appearance at a rally on Sunday. He wasn’t wearing a timepiece at all, surprisingly. Which meant that there, on his wrist, was the mark of a true collector: a watch tan.

#6726. A New Marni x Hoka Sneaker Is Almost Here—Here’s What to Know

The Italian fashion house once again brings its unique touch to the athletic brand.

Last year, when Marni and Hoka launched their first collaboration, the two labels came together to bring the world a collection of puffy, chunky, candy-colored takes on the athletic footwear brand’s Bondi sneaker. Naturally, it was a hit among the streetwear set, including the likes of Steph Curry. Of course, a lot can change in the span of a year and a half—and the latest sneaker trends are no exception. In the same way jeans have gone from baggy styles to straight-leg and even skinny jeans, fashion has taken its sneakers from their dad eras to silhouettes that lean a little sleeker. The latest result of these turning tides: The Hoka Clifton Marni.

“Shifting from the maximalist and oversized aesthetic towards a calmer, more essential form made sense with Meryll [Rogge]’s ascension to Marni,” Thomas Cykana, Hoka’s senior director of global collaborations, tells ELLE in an email. “This affords a simple but surprising design that cues premium embellishments, metallic hardware, and unexpected prints over an overtly in-your-face design. This shift enables consumers to both craft their uniform and express their individuality without sacrificing Hoka’s pure performance capabilities.”

Launching globally on November 13, the design is the culmination of form and function. Marni brings its unique design perspective to the technical shoe, not only with the chosen colors—Orange, Black, and White—but also with design-forward touches such as woven heel tabs, windowpane-patterned insoles, and three shoelace options for each colorway.

“Marni has a unique ability to take everyday design cues and make them feel artful and unexpected. That lust for curiosity and imaginative nature is what first drew our team to the label and continues to inspire us,” Cykana shares. “Our debut collection in 2025 showed how much our teams share in creativity and craftsmanship, and that trust led us to our unique spin on the iconic Clifton. The editorial tone they delivered to this project reflects the perfect sensation of everyday and extraordinary at once.”

The Hoka Clifton Marni sneaker will be available for $275 on November 13 at Hoka.com and select global retailers.

Is Levi Alves McConaughey Hollywood’s next rising star to know? Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves’s eldest son turned 18 earlier this year and seems to be following in his father’s footsteps, gradually stepping into his own spotlight.

Over the years, Levi has joined his famous parents on red carpets and at industry events, most recently at last night’s Airbnb.Org Gala in Los Angeles, where he even had his own solo moment on the red carpet. With two acting credits, a runway debut, and several Fashion Week appearances under his belt, he’s beginning to build a public persona of his own. And in the world of celebrity offspring, all signs certainly point to a career in the making for Levi.

Here’s everything to know about the young McConaughey, who’s just getting started.

Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves McConaughey welcomed their first child, Levi Alves McConaughey, on July 7, 2008. He’s the eldest of the Hollywood couple’s three children. They also share a daughter, Vida (born in 2010), and a son, Livingston (born in 2012).

Over the years, Matthew has spoken about the importance of instilling a strong work ethic in his three children. During a 2020 appearance at The History Channel’s HISTORYTalks, the actor called his kids his “living legacy” and said he taught them the value of hard work by giving them small jobs on his sets.

“I have my kids come out, we put them to work,” the Dazed and Confused star said. “We give them a little cash for catering.”

Levi has also joined his parents in giving back. In 2023, Alves brought Levi and daughter Vida to Refettorio Paris, where they helped cook and serve meals to people in need. Levi later reflected on the experience in an Instagram post, writing, “I got the chance to cook at @refettorioparis for some people that don’t normally get to have a really nice meal. Refettorio Paris serves first class meals to the homeless. They made a great restaurant with high-end chefs to cook—using produce that was going to be thrown away.”

He added, “It was really cool to serve some people that don’t normally get to have it.”

Levi made his acting debut in the 2025 film The Lost Bus, starring opposite his father. The up-and-coming actor plays Shaun McKay, the son of Kevin McKay, who is portrayed by his real-life dad.

But as he tried out for the role. Levi didn’t want his famous last name to give him a leg up. In an interview with People, the father-son duo revealed that Levi auditioned for the role anonymously, with his last name removed so he could earn the part all on his own.

“Can you pull the last name?” Matthew asked the film’s casting director. “She goes, ‘Yeah.’ And I got a call back and she said, ‘Our director Paul Greengrass said, ‘That’s the kid. That’s the son, Levi.’ And then she goes, and ‘I told him that’s actually Matthew’s son in real life.’”

For Levi, the role was an opportunity to explore his interest in acting. “This role wasn’t me going, ‘Oh, I’m going to become an actor,’ It was me saying, ‘I’m really interested in this.’”

Levi has entered the fashion scene on a few occasions, including sitting front row at the Dior Homme Spring 2026 show during Paris Fashion Week.

He also made his official catwalk debut during Milan Fashion Week this season, walking the Vogue World runway.

In 2025, Levi opened up to Interview magazine about his mom, dad, and budding Hollywood career. The teen shared why he idolizes both of his parents: “My dad for the man he is, because of the work he has been able to create, and how he’s handled it all,” he said. “My mom for the woman she is, her patience, and her want to help others.”

When asked if he wanted to be famous, he said, “Famous in a lasting way. I want to continue to build on a legacy that I have the privilege to carry on.”

#6723. The Met Gala 2027 Theme “extraORDINARY,” Explained

Love jeans and t-shirts? This one’s for you.

Today, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that its spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition and Met Gala will be devoted to familiar garments and commonplace materials rendered remarkable via the interventions of designers. Organized by Curator in Charge Andrew Bolton, with assistance from Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben, the Met Gala 2027 theme, “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” will ask its visitors “to see the everyday anew.” It will come at its subject from two directions, one focusing on the elevation of archetypal garments, i.e. the above-mentioned tees and jeans, and the the other examining how humble, even “disposable” materials, from paper to aluminum to plastic, are transformed into wearable art.

The exhibition replaces the John Galliano blockbuster originally planned for 2027 that was subsequently canceled after it became a cultural flashpoint.

“I didn’t have a plan B,” Bolton says candidly. “It was really important to come up with an exhibition that wasn’t just a masterwork show or something that we could do a little bit more easily. I wanted it to be as challenging and as provocative and as beautiful as a John show would have been.” He continues: “That was really important to me: to come up with an idea that wasn’t a substitute. And it had to have some sort of contemporary resonance.”

Bolton went back to “Costume Art,” the Costume Institute’s 2026 show as a starting point. That exhibition “placed the dressed body at the center of aesthetic experience,” he says, “and I suppose it led me to think more about how we experience clothing in everyday life through habit and touch and movement and sensation.”

Pieces from Jun Takahashi’s fall 2024 Undercover show will greet guests at the entrance to “extraORDINARY.”

The final gallery will feature the work of Anrealage’s Kuniko Moringa.

Both of these pieces are from the fall 2024 Anrealage collection.

In that sense, “extraORDINARY” dovetails with a movement across the recent fashion shows in which designers embraced real, recognizable clothes and platformed individuality—soul, you could even call it—via their styling. “Quiet gestures hold so much more meaning than the louder gestures,” Bolton says. “Bravado—we should be looking at the opposite of that.”

He was drawn in particular to the Japanese designer Jun Takahashi’s fall 2024 Undercover collection, a sublimely moving show that was inspired by Wim Wenders’s contemplative film about the beauty of everyday life, Perfect Days, and included a spoken poem specially written for the occasion by the director about the daily rituals of a single mother, “Watching a Working Woman.” Garments from Takahashi’s collection—otherwise unremarkable pieces reworked via collage and layering techniques that rendered them anything but prosaic—will greet visitors at the entrance to “extraORDINARY.” They “give the exhibition a real human starting point,” Bolton says.

The show will close with the work of another Japanese designer, Anrealage’s Kunihiko Morinaga, whose “unfamiliar geometries” and “unexpected proportions” add a conceptual dimension to what is otherwise familiar. Rain parkas and trench coats as “objects of wonder.”

Jonathan Anderson’s Loewe, spring 2022 ready-to-wear

Moncler 1 by Pierpaolo Piccioli, fall 2019

Helmut Lang, spring 1993. (Photo by Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

In between, “Familiar Forms” will look more closely at designers’ interventions of common items—Virgil Abloh’s Off-White t-shirts, Gianfranco Ferré’s demonstrative white shirts, trenches from Jonathan Anderson at Loewe and “the different designers at Burberry,” and puffer gowns from Pierpaolo Piccioli’s collections for Moncler all of which, one way of the other, “put the extra in the ordinary,” Bolton says.

“Common Matter,” meanwhile, will delve into the potential of throwaway materials and found objects as actual garments. Margiela will be prominent in this gallery, alongside other designers who have made a habit of repurposing materials. “A paper dress,” Bolton says, can demand as much skill and as much labor as a silk gown. And the cost of a material tells us very little about the craftsmanship required to transform it. Reuse and reconstruction run through the exhibition because I’m interested in how things acquire life and how that changes what we value and care for.”

A dress made from paper. Comme des Garçons, spring 1992 ready-to-wear

A silverware bodice. Maison Margiela, spring 2027 ready-to-wear

Questions of value, consumption, and resourcefulness give the exhibition a particular urgency, Bolton feels. “It will make us question: what do we overlook, what do we discard, what makes something worth keeping?” I think that fashion is so often associated with the pursuit of the new and the ephemeral that I’m really interested in how possibilities can emerge through returning to familiar things. I think there’s something hopeful about discovering how much imagination the everyday can hold.”

If that doesn’t have the promise of Galliano’s fantastic and radical reimaginings, it is not merely the humdrum we’ll be talking about. Among the pieces bound to amuse and delight are a splintered china ensemble from Martin Margiela and Ellen Hodakova Larsson’s next-generation jangly spoon dress.

Jeans and a cotton tank that aren’t really jeans and a cotton tank, but leather. From Matthieu Blazy’s Bottega Veneta debut for fall 2022.

The exhibition, which opens to the public on May 9, 2027 after the Met Gala on May 3 and will be on view through January 9, 2028, is being conceptualized by the London-based scenographic design studio, 1009, with the intention of creating a dialogue between the installation and the people that will move among it. “I want the visitors to be part of the exhibition,” Bolton says. In fact, if he had his way, the show itself, not just the red carpet ball that precedes it, would have a dress code. He likes the idea of people wearing “their favorite t-shirt or their favorite pair of jeans or their favorite hoodie” as they navigate their way through the show. “There’ll be a humanity to it,” he says.

“extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will be sponsored by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler, and additional support from Condé Nast. Education programs presented in conjunction with the exhibition are made possible by Jordan Roth.

A Junya Watanabe fall 2011 biker will be showcased in the “Familiar Forms” room.

#6721. The Best Men’s Rain Boots Ranked From Drizzle to Downpour

The best rain boots for men aren’t a one-size-fits-all shoe. The chance of precipitation may be 100%, but you could be stepping out to a gentle mist, wading through cataclysmic flooding, or taking on sporadic showers—so your choice of shoes and outerwear should adapt to the weather. Popping up out for a quick coffee could require a pair of simple gardening shoes or tall wellingtons depending on whether you’re walking a few blocks or taking your car to a drive-thru.

There are many factors to consider but the most important is that your feet and socks remain dry, no matter the shoe or how heavy the rain is. So take into consideration how tall or short your rain boot ought to be, whether you need grippy soles to get you through some rough terrain or you might have to contend with slush and snow, which inevitably means you’ll need some boots with insulation. Your rain boots and shoes have to contend with a litany of different factors so we rounded up the best options for every kind of wet-weather situation from mild mists to ankle-deep downpours.

For the kind of mediocre rain that has you second-guessing whether you should open your umbrella or just stick it out, you’ll likely get by just fine with a pair of shoes built with a water-resistant or waterproof membrane. Think a slight spray or an annoying mist. Many outdoors-focused shoes and boots come with some type of Gore-tex lining or a coating that helps slough light water. In mild rain situations, your shoes don’t need to be very tall, either. Low-cut gardening shoes or rain-ready sneakers can manage the weather just so long as there’s a low risk of deep puddles along the way.

Norda's trail-ready slip-on runners are an iron-clad pick for any rocky terrain you might encounter, purposely or not. With their lightweight, tear- and water-resistant Dyneema uppers, and crag-grabbing Vibram lugged soles, these bad boys can handle more than a drizzle. Plus, the easy slip-on design is great for when you just need to jam out the door for a quick errand, not to mention for keeping water from sogging your socks.

If the precipitation falls anywhere between a drizzle to moderate showers, I can’t be arsed to bust out my heavier rain boots. I’m unlikely to wear my wellies in showers, too, if I know I won’t be outside for too long. For most situations, a good water-resistant boot will more than suffice. Save your brain cells and just get a pair of Blundstones—they’re tough as nails, reliably dry in the majority of rainy days, and look great with any pant. But if boots on the wellies-chelsea spectrum aren’t your speed, there are plenty of other shoes with rain-prepped details like Gore-tex linings and DWR coatings to keep water at bay.

It's hard to argue against a pair of Blundstones. The quality leather uppers age beautifully, the shape is ruggedly handsome and endlessly styleable, plus the hardy soles can handle most everyday situations regardless of the forecast. No wonder why you see everyone from your local barista to Hollywood's leading men rocking a pair. Their waterproof design is adept at traversing through medium rain, so long as you don't step into any deep puddles, and we like that they don't present as a full-on rubber boot which makes them easier to wear all year long.

What you’re probably imagining when you think of proper rain boots are the kind wrought entirely out of a block of rubber, reaching up to your calf, without any laces. Some people refer to these as Wellingtons—or wellies—whose origins go back to the Duke of Wellington, and though they were originally made of leather, are now mostly thought of as a rain-ready boot. Their seamless, monoblock design in conjunction with impermeable rubber makes them the right choice for heavy rain or if you plan on being outside for several hours in average rainfall conditions. Of course, they’re well-equipped for lighter precipitation as well.

Hunter's flagship boots are a textbook Wellington rain boot. Made entirely of waterproof (not water-resistant) rubber from sole to shaft, no amount of rain, sludge, or slush penetrates these boots. The carved rubber soles keep their grip amidst slippery sidewalks and slick metal grates, while the height is tall enough to stand nice and dry through calf-deep water, but isn't so tall to be a physical or stylistic burden. And at just under $200, they're a reasonable price for the quality.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6719. The 2027 Met Gala Theme Could Bring Jeans and T-Shirts to Fashion’s Biggest Night

“Extraordinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” examines the clothes we wear on repeat.

Alas, the 2027 Met Gala has a new theme after the Costume Institute scrapped its planned John Galliano exhibition. Titled “Extraordinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” the show turns its attention to the clothes and materials we might otherwise overlook and what designers can make of them. The gala takes place May 3, with the exhibition opening to the public six days later. It’s a marked shift from the theatrical world of Galliano’s designs and could mean that we see jeans and (gasp!) T-shirts in droves during the biggest night in fashion.

Here, everything to know about the 2027 Met Gala theme, dress code, and more.

The dress code has yet to be announced. It will take its cue from the exhibition, as is tradition, but what that means for the red carpet remains to be seen. “I want visitors to leave looking differently at the clothes they arrived in,” Andrew Bolton, curator in charge of the Costume Institute, said in a statement of the exhibit. “With a greater sense of what is worth noticing, valuing, and caring for.”

Each year, the Met Gala’s dress code gives guests a way to interpret the Costume Institute’s spring exhibition. The 2027 prompt has yet to be announced, but the show’s focus on everyday clothing and materials—from jeans and T-shirts to paper, aluminum, and plastic—offers plenty of clues.

The exhibition will bring together over 200 pieces, roughly a third from the museum’s collection and the rest on loan or donated. Among them: Charles James’s ’30s couture puffer coat; pieces from Marc Jacobs’s grunge-era Perry Ellis collections; Brooke Shields’s Calvin Klein jeans, made famous by the brand’s 1980 ad; Junya Watanabe’s take on the leather biker jacket, filtered through the codes of Dior’s New Look; and Matthieu Blazy’s trompe l’oeil leather “jeans” for Bottega Veneta. The show will also include pieces that have been upcycled, recycled, and otherwise remade.

Despite the pomp and circumstance of the event, everyday dressing is already embedded in the Met Gala lexicon. At the 2026 gala, Bhavitha Mandava slipped into silk jeans and a three-quarter zip-up by Chanel; Kim Kardashian wore a head-to-toe Balenciaga T-shirt dress in 2021; and Doja Cat took the idea further in a wet-look Vetements tee dress in 2024. For 2027, expect the eventual dress code to invite that same kind of transformation: familiar pieces, reworked for the red carpet.

The 2027 gala’s hosts have not yet been announced.

#6716. Can You Manifest a Husband?

This spring, singer Natalie Imbruglia joined Elizabeth Day on her How to Fail podcast to discuss, among other things, how she manifested her husband. The clip predictably made the rounds online, and it got me thinking about the mechanics of calling in a partner. It’s easy enough to enchant your life with inspirational buzzwords, but sometimes the spell lacks teeth—or worse, you attract someone who matches your checklist on paper but operates on an entirely different wavelength. (You asked for a multilingual finance professional who loves dogs; the universe delivered an auditor who speaks Latin and brought three untamed Dobermans to drinks.)

Pop culture has taken note. On The Kardashians, Kim revealed she learned manifestation techniques from Michael Jackson to draw in aligned suitors, while Khloé echoed the sentiment, treating it as a baseline tool to shape the dynamic she wants. Been there, done that. To cut through the noise, I turned to practicing experts—happily partnered, naturally—for the real rituals and energetic groundwork required to call in a mate.

For many, myself included, previous attempts at manifesting love hit speed bumps: the timing was off, or the wish list wasn't nearly specific enough—ask the universe for someone “adventurous and spontaneous,” and you might end up conjuring an unemployed DJ who doesn’t own a bed frame. In Day’s case, her mother’s friend Lizzie advised her to write down her romantic non-negotiables in ink, then burn the page to release the intention to the universe. It worked—eventually. Magic is an iterative sport, requiring trial, error, and honest self-assessment. Here is what my coven of experts suggests.

The starting point is radical specificity. “Sit down and have a conversation with your heart,” advises astrologer Narayana Montufar, author of Written in Your Stars. She recommends taking pen to paper to define what a true life partner looks like, stripped of outside expectations. “Most of us carry preconceived notions about what marriage is, which may not even be ours,” she explains. Because the universe responds to energetic resonance rather than superficial wish lists, your birth chart can provide a clear roadmap: “Look at your Moon sign for nurturance, your Venus sign for attraction, and your Mars sign for sexual chemistry.”

Equally crucial is auditing past missteps. Astrologer Renee Watt urges taking stock of where prior relationships unraveled and what red flags were brushed aside. “It's possible you've prioritized traits that are ‘sexy’ over qualities that actually contribute to sustainable connections,” she notes, emphasizing that unaddressed jealousy, passivity, or fear will sabotage even the most celestial match. “Once you've gained a strong awareness of what you no longer wish to carry or attract, banish it.”

Once the mental slate is clear, ritual grounds the intention. Corbin Chamberlin, founder of Sage & Salt perfumery, recommends beginning on a Friday—traditionally Venus’s day of love. “Take a cleansing salt bath,” he suggests. “Afterward, write down the qualities you want to receive in a marriage, then the qualities you’re prepared to give in return.” Fold the page toward you three times, place it beneath a white candle, and recite: ‘I make space for a love I can recognize, receive, and return.’ Chamberlin also emphasizes backing magic up with physical space: clear a drawer, a nightstand, or a section of closet to signal you have room for another person in your life.

For astrologer Lauren Ash, intentional jewelry serves as a daily talisman. “Marriage is about much more than jewelry, but a ring is something you see and feel throughout the day,” she says. Different fingers govern different planetary energies: the thumb aligns with Mars for bold initiative; the index finger channels Jupiter for expansion; and the middle finger invokes Saturn for structure and enduring commitment. “The hand matters, too,” Ash adds. “The right hand is what you’re putting out into the world, and the left is what you’re inviting in. You could wear rose quartz on your right ring finger to signal receptivity, and a stone tied to your ideal partner’s Sun or Venus on your left.”

To bolster your environment, Watt recommends burning pink candles for affection, incorporating stones like rhodochrosite and green aventurine, or wearing essential oils of rose and geranium. Montufar also suggests syncing visual meditations with the New Moon, capitalizing on its monthly cycle of clean slates and quiet momentum.

Yet every practitioner shares the same non-negotiable caveat: the real work happens internally before any match arrives. “Before you do the ritual to call in a partner, do the ritual for yourself,” Chamberlin cautions. “We spend so much time thinking about what we want to attract, but very little thinking about our capacity to receive and maintain it. Manifestation isn’t just asking for something—it’s preparing yourself for its arrival.”

That preparation often means shedding rigid aesthetics. “Keep an open mind,” Watt advises, noting that fixating on identical tastes in music or film can blind you to a genuine connection. “My husband holds very little resemblance to any fantasies I once carried in my head, but he's consistent, supportive, and makes me laugh. Before he came into the picture, what I thought I wanted didn't align with what I actually needed.”

At its core, calling in a partner demands unshakeable confidence in the outcome and the emotional stability to hold space for them when they arrive. As Montufar points out, trust is the real engine behind attraction: the clearer your belief that the universe is tuned in, the sharper the results. I’ve previously manifested the exact right match on paper only to watch it collapse because I lacked the grounding to sustain it. Doing the internal homework is where the actual sorcery begins. Happy manifesting, witches.
