#6715. 13 Best Deodorant for Men 2026, According to Dermatologists

Frankly, the best deodorant for men sells itself. It stinks to stink: Body odor is right up there with bad breath as a totally avoidable misfortune. But while deodorant might seem like an odd category to get overly psyched about, as a longtime grooming editor, I can confidently say we're living in a golden age of the underarm essential.

Unlike the synthetic and chalky ghosts of deodorant sticks past, today’s best deodorants are a a sea of sophisticated formulas, improved textures, better scents, and naturally derived ingredients that, yes, actually work. The only hard part is honing in on the best one for you. Price, feel, skin sensitivity, and your sweat and odor levels matter. So I tested a whole lot of deodorants to narrow the field to seven standouts, some new, some tried-and-true, plus a few more deeper cuts I also loved.

I also tapped trusted dermatologists, for some expert insights further down. Just one last quick note: We’re not talking antiperspirants here, which primarily rely on aluminum compounds to reduce sweat. If that’s what you’re after, I’ve got recommendations for those, too.

Now, are there more targeted, more sophisticated, and, well, chicer deodorants on this list? Absolutely. But at the end of the day, you want your deo to do three things: keep the stink at bay, smell good, and be easy to repurchase. Dove Men+Care hits every mark, which is why it's in every drugstore.

The price, of course, is great, but then there's the scent: a surprisingly sophisticated blend of bright bergamot and warm white amber that's fresh, subtly citrusy, and softly warm. It smells so much better than your typical underarm fare and is actually a little mood-boosting, as the packaging suggests. The aluminum-free, baking-soda-free formula features moisture-attracting ingredients, giving it a little skincare credibility, too. It also feels super smooth going on, and kept its scent for most of the day. No notes!

Hip grooming brand Church California's deodorant only launched two years ago, but for me, it's everything a niche, forward-thinking deodorant should be: Effective, made with almost entirely naturally derived ingredients, and housed in compostable, plastic-free packaging. The formula uses magnesium and organic tapioca starch for odor and moisture control, with coconut oil and shea butter adding a little skin-conditioning goodness. And that scent? Wonderfully herbaceous, thanks to an essential oil blend that smells like the actual outdoors.

Admittedly, the sturdy cardboard tube takes a little getting used to—you push the stick up from the bottom instead of twisting a dial. And the glide is certainly a little less smooth. But oh, does the formula hold up. Even hours later, I'd catch little whiffs of those lovely botanicals, and when the scent eventually faded, there was still no detectable B.O. For the environmentally conscious guy, it's a no-brainer, and for the aesthete, it looks retro cool sitting on your medicine cabinet shelf.

Ursa Major’s Hoppin’ Fresh stick is a modern legend in the deo space. Among us grooming geeks, this au naturel-meets-elevated formula changed the underarm game when it launched in 2015. It was one of those early artisanal step-ups from drugstore fare, and it earned the hype with thoughtfully curated, foraged-sounding ingredients, a subtle, natural-smelling citrus scent, and a skincare-centric stick that glides on smoothly.

It still holds up today, fighting odor, soothing skin, and absorbing excess moisture to keep you smelling fresh. For an aluminum-free deo, it also keeps me pretty dry, too. And even the packaging—a sleek, solid-blue tube—feels like a style upgrade. Scent wise, in winter Forest Fix is the way to go. But the original Hoppin' Fresh is always waiting in the wings once the warmer months come around.

I'm well aware that Old Spice has plenty of newer, more fragrance-centric variations, many with names like Swagger. But I've always preferred the tried-and-true stuff, and that blue stick, here in High Endurance Refresh, is about as iconic as deodorant gets. It's my old reliable, and one I always keep as a backup, whether I'm visiting family, staying overnight somewhere, or just need something I can count on in a pinch. This classic has aged remarkably well, because it simply works.

Then there's the nostalgia, which hits me every time I catch a whiff of that distinctively fresh-meets-medicinal aroma I've loved unironically for years. The formula isn't particularly fancy: science-y ingredients give the aluminum-free stick its smooth glide, while glycerin adds a little skin-conditioning benefit. Would I wear this for an Ironman competition? Probably not. But for everyday errands, workdays, and just about everything in between? Absolutely. At under $15 for a three-pack, it's also easily one of the best value options on this list.

When you think gel deodorant, you probably picture those old-school perforated dispensers with tons of holes. But Baxter of California's is a smooth, transparent gel stick that's still, in my book, among the best. Part of the appeal is the formula, which packs some impressive botanicals: witch hazel and tea tree oil help tackle odor-causing bacteria, while chamomile helps soothe skin. Add tried-and-true glycerin to the mix, and you've got a gel deodorant with some serious skincare cred, too.

Then there's the application itself. The clear gel glides on effortlessly, with a cool, crisp, almost medicinal feel that's especially refreshing during the warmer months. Better still, it won't leave white marks on your shirts, something I always appreciate with my go-to black T-shirts. Is it the most heavy-duty odor fighter on this list? Not quite. But for everyday wear, it keeps the funk at bay without feeling like you've applied much of anything.

I test a lot of deodorants, but few become permanent fixtures in my bathroom. So it's worth telling you that Freaks of Nature's Everyday Endurance has become my primary deodorant lately. The brand may be known best for sunscreen, but it knows its way around our underarms too. And much like its sunscreens, part of the appeal is the application. The lotion-like formula emerges through a clever F-shaped grate, and there's something oddly satisfying about watching it dispense before smoothing it onto your underarms.

Better still, it absorbs well without any gunky, sticky residue. Cocoa butter and sunflower oil give it a skin-conditioning quality that makes this one of the most soothing deodorants I've ever worn. It's premium-priced, sure, but between the standout application, exemplary performance, and skin-conditioning feel, it's worth every penny.

Gone are the days when deodorant had to smell like “Sports Ice Rush.” Today's best odor fighters offer sophisticated, subtle scents (so they don't compete with your cologne), and Salt & Stone remains one of the top examples, with deodorants that have actual scent pyramids—Saffron & Cedar, Black Rose & Oud, Bergamot & Hinoki, for example. All are nuanced, refined, and never too loud.

But it's not just about the scent. The formula neutralizes odor and absorbs excess moisture very well, while skincare-centric additions like niacinamide and shea butter help keep underarms comfortable. More importantly, in my experience, the fragrance doesn't devolve into some funky olfactory murk by day's end. You still smell like the scent you applied that morning, or at the very least, fresh. Are these the heaviest-duty or most affordable deodorants out there? Nope. But they deliver on fragrance and function, and that's a combination worth investing in.

Caldera Lab just launched its first deodorant, and given the brand's skincare chops, it's no surprise the formula reads like a serum: niacinamide, aloe vera, and hyaluronic acid soothe and hydrate; postbiotics and magnesium tackle odor; and arrowroot absorbs moisture. Stacked, indeed.

Can Aesop do any wrong? Not really, and its deodorant spray is another example of the botanical-meets-aromatic goodness the amber-hued brand does so well. It's the only spray on this list, and while its odor protection holds up well, a midday refresh is sometimes warranted—and honestly, part of the pleasure.

If your skin is extra sensitive, Nécessaire's entire fragrance-free lineup is exemplary, and its deodorant stick is no exception. It keeps odor impressively in check, is easy on sensitive underarms, and won't compete with your favorite cologne. It's also aluminum- and baking soda-free, dermatologist-tested, hypoallergenic, and even carries the National Eczema Association's Seal of Acceptance.

Cremo may be kings of shave cream, but it knows a thing or two about deodorant, too. The formulas are affordable, the odor protection holds up, and the scents smell so damn good. Take Palo Santo, with its warm, woody, slightly smoky aroma that feels far more sophisticated than its price suggests. Coconut oil and shea butter add the skin-conditioning touch you'd expect from a pricier stick. rant quietly in the background, look elsewhere—but if you like a lot of fragrance with your funk-fighting, Cremo delivers serious bang for the buck.

The Grey's culty, rightfully hyped deodorant is the best old-school-style roll-on I've ever tried. The unscented formula is so lightweight you almost have to check you're applying anything, but oh, you are, and there's a cooling tingle as it goes on. It's the most expensive deodorant on this list, but with its premium slim aluminum casing and impressively lightweight formula, it's an investment in barely-there odor-fighting care.

Malin+Goetz's Eucalyptus Deodorant is a stone-cold classic that helped elevate gel sticks and make them feel refreshingly natural. The scent is practically a trademark at this point, equal parts medicinal, herbal, and oh-so-subtle. But there's substance behind it: eucalyptus extract helps refresh skin, while odor-neutralizing citronellyl methylcrotonate keeps the funk at bay.

As a grooming editor, I've tried more sticks, sprays, gels, and roll-ons than I can count, from drugstore staples to niche newcomers. And while plenty have impressed me on first swipe, the real test is whether I keep reaching for them weeks, months, or even years later.

Here, I drew on firsthand testing, focusing on odor protection, scent, texture, application, skin comfort, and, of course, how well they hold up. I've worn these deodorants through warm and cool weather, long days, and everything in between. Some are favorites I've relied on for years, while others are newer that are now part of my medicine cabinet rotation. As I've said, the best deodorant sometimes depends on the occasion or even the season, so it's a good idea to have a few on hand if possible. At the end of the day, a deodorant needs to keep B.O. at bay, ideally absorb excess moisture, and feel comfortable. Some excel in certain areas more than others, but each one above warrants its spot among the best deodorants.

Here is some dermatologist advice on deodorants—the best ingredients to look for, plus some controversial ones, too—with insights from board-certified dermatologists Kiran Mian, Ryan B. Turner, and Heather Rogers.

The primary cause of body odor is “bad” bacteria pairing up with sweat. There are two ways to prevent the stink: Reduce perspiration in the area, and/or create an inhospitable environment for the bacteria.

These are the most common ingredients to seek out if you want to temper the proliferation of bacteria in your pits (and anywhere you’re particularly pungent).

This antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory mineral safely and effectively kills bacteria without irritating skin, says Mian.

Dr. Mian also endorses the non-irritating magnesium hydroxide, a naturally occurring compound that neutralizes bacteria without absorbing into the skin.

“The terpenes in tea tree oil make this ingredient naturally antibacterial and antifungal, helping to reduce body odor,” Turner says. “In its pure, concentrated form, it can be very irritating. It’s best to use a product that’s formulated with tea tree oil at low percentages. It’s still effective when diluted, and a little bit goes a very long way.”

This one is controversial to some. Most skin types will tolerate baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) just fine, but only trust reputable, well-reviewed brands who use it. “Baking soda has a very alkaline pH level, while that of the skin is more acidic,” explains Turner. “This disrupts the skin’s natural barrier, harming the good bacteria in our microbiome, and leaving our skin more susceptible to irritation and inflammation.” (We’ve included a few deodorants with baking soda below, plus many natural picks that explicitly exclude it.)

It’s easy to get these two confused, but they share a principle. “Prebiotics feed the good bacteria on our skin (bacteria that does not break down sweat releasing a foils odor), which then overpopulates those odor-producing bacteria,” explains Mian. “Probiotics are the good bacteria that will ideally populate the skin and overtake odor causing bacteria.” The names of these might be strange to you, like lactobacillus acidophilus or saccharomyces ferment. Chances are, a brand will proudly tout their pre- and probiotics, so look for that indication instead.

“These chemical exfoliating ingredients help resurface the skin, which also strips away bacteria as well as removes the dead skin that bacteria break down, which causes body odor,” says Turner. And Dr. Rogers echoes the love: “Using acids to exfoliate the skin in our armpits helps rebuild the acidic mantle [which is compromised with age], leading to better control of bacterial growth and odor. Many acids work great; glycolic, lactic acid and mandelic acid are my favorites. Salicylic acid, a beta hydroxy acid, has a higher chance of irritation.”

“Activated charcoal can help to absorb sweat and help to neutralize odors,” says Turner.

Arrowroot powder, tapioca starch, and cornstarch are popular ingredients in aluminum-free deodorants, helping absorb excess moisture and keep underarms feeling dry without blocking sweat production. Of tapioca starch, Mian says, “This non-irritating starch won’t clog sweat ducts like aluminum, which can cause breakouts.” (It's also terrific in anti-chafe products for similar moisture-absorbing benefits.) “Like tapioca starch, corn starch pulls moisture from the skin to leave a powdery feeling behind. Unless you have an allergy to these plants, they are safer to use,” says Turner. Both doctors particularly favor arrowroot powder as a naturally derived, generally well-tolerated ingredient for absorbing moisture.

Both help soak up surface moisture without blocking sweat production. Freaks of Nature's formula includes bentonite clay.

A naturally occurring, porous mineral powder that absorbs excess moisture and helps keep underarms dry. You'll find it in Ursa Major's deodorant.

Approach your deodorant purchase with the following considerations:

While it’s easy to celebrate a fully natural formula—and for good reason—keep in mind that not all natural ingredients are inherently good for your skin. Ingredients like baking soda and certain essential oils can cause irritation, particularly if your underarms are sensitive. Conversely, synthetic ingredients aren't automatically bad for your skin, either. “What’s more important is to consider the manufacturer of the products—are they reputable? Do they perform extensive testing? What are the ingredients used and from where are they sourced?” says Turner. That's sound advice whether you're shopping natural or synthetic. There's a reason dermatologists frequently recommend established brands like Dove: They have the resources to develop, test, and manufacture formulas at scale, often at a fraction of the price of more niche alternatives. Of course, that doesn't mean smaller brands aren't doing their homework, either. Finding the right deodorant still takes some trial and error, gents, but you can always start with our list.

If your underarms are easily irritated, start with the ingredient list. Baking soda, strong fragrances, essential oils, and certain acids can trigger irritation, though everyone's skin reacts differently. Look for skin-conditioning ingredients like shea butter, glycerin, and aloe, several of which you'll find in the deodorants featured above. Fragrance-free formulas are a smart starting point for sensitive skin, while unscented are worth considering, too—just know that some contain masking fragrances.

Deodorants come in all sorts of formats these days, from classic solid sticks and clear gels to sprays, roll-ons, lotions, and pastes. How they feel when you apply them matters as much as how well they work. Some glide on more smoothly, while others feel chalkier, thicker, or more moisturizing. Gels and roll-ons tend to feel lightweight and refreshing (great for warmer weather), while richer lotions and pastes feel more nourishing and suit the cooler months. Ultimately, the best deodorant feels comfortable, doesn't leave residue on your clothes, and fits your lifestyle.

Dr. Kiran Mian is a board-certified dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology and Laser Surgery in NYC, and volunteer faculty at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai University.

Dr. Ryan B. Turner is a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Turner Dermatology in NYC and the TRNR Skin skin care line.

Dr. Heather Rogers is a board-certified dermatologist and co-founder of Modern Dermatology in Seattle and the founder of the Doctor Rogers skin care line.

#6712. Three New Fragrances That Guarantee “You Smell Good” Compliments

Contrapposto is the latest brainchild of a beauty industry hitmaker

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

You know when someone smells so good it stops you in your tracks? I ran into a friend recently and spent our entire conversation trying not to make it obvious how distracted her scent made me. Part of the intrigue was that I couldn’t quite place what I was smelling. It was unmistakably floral, but its elusiveness made it all the more magnetic. She was wearing Melting Flowers by Contrapposto.

In sculpture, contrapposto describes the shift in a figure’s weight that gives the body a sense of natural movement. Italian for “counterpoise,” it’s also the name of Nécessaire, Homecourt, and Into the Gloss co-founder and former Elle and WWD editor Nick Axelrod-Welk’s latest venture.

Founded with his husband, Casey Welk, in 2023, Contrapposto began as an aesthetic dermatology practice in West Hollywood and has since expanded into fine fragrance, with its first collection launching this fall. On the surface, the aesthetics and scent might seem worlds apart. But as Nick explains in our conversation ahead, the move reflects a deliberate vision for what he wants Contrapposto to become.

What really connected the clinic and the product for me was this idea of enhancing rather than transforming: enhancing your skin, the way you smell, and the way you feel, rather than turning you into someone else. That became kind of the battle cry for the brand.

I also loved the challenge of fragrance. It's such a subjective category. There's no before and after, no claims. Either you like it, or you don't. And I saw a white space in luxury fragrance, where the more you spend, the more you're expected to project and have people notice your scent. I wanted to do something different.

I wanted to introduce scents that melt into your skin and enhance the way you smell and feel. Because I think the only reason to put something into the world in 2026 is to truly add pleasure to someone’s life.

They’re really meant to be experienced on skin. All of the fragrances are quite heavy in musks and lactones, which are molecules that are very dynamic on skin, so the fragrances come alive when you wear them. They can smell different from what you might expect on paper, too. Someone might think they’d never wear a floral fragrance, for example, but then try Melting Flowers and discover this creamy, addictive, woody, sandalwood base that makes them reconsider.

I wouldn’t call them subtle skin scents, though. These are big fragrances that project. They just have this ability to impart a coziness that I love in all my fragrances.

I approach everything by asking, “Who are the best people in this field?” When I started thinking about creating fragrance, I took a step back and thought about the launches that had made a real impact on me when I was an editor. The one I still think about is Tom Ford Private Blend. I remember seeing it at Barneys or Bergdorf Goodman in New York. The amber bottles and the olfactive profiles. These dark woods, ouds, and leathers were new to a Western audience at the time, and yet there was something inherently addictive and commercial about the scents. They were likable.

That was the balance I wanted to strike with Contrapposto: something new and unique that doesn’t smell like anything else, but also has this inherent commerciality to it—something so appealing that it invites as many people to the party as possible.

I knew fragrance was its own world, with its own language, and that if I wasn’t the expert, I needed to find the expert. My job was to find the right people and get them excited about what I was trying to create, so we could do it together. This led me to Karyn Khoury, who had been instrumental in developing Private Blend during her time at Estée Lauder. But Karyn had retired in 2019, moved to Florida, and wasn’t exactly looking to be found.

Long story short, I was able to reach her through a mutual connection, and over the course of a year, we slowly got to know each other. I had her smell what I had been working on and eventually convinced her to become an advisor for me.

Karyn also introduced me to Shyamala Maisondieu [a master perfumer at Givaudan], and we immediately clicked. She’s the kind of person who lives with the fragrances she’s creating. She wears them on her own skin and pays attention to how they evolve. While developing Musc Pétille, she texted me from vacation to say it was finally complete because someone stopped her to ask what she was wearing.

I knew Frank from interviewing him for my podcast, Eyewitness Beauty, several years earlier. What I quickly realized is that getting a meeting with these master perfumers is one thing, but getting them genuinely excited about what you’re doing is a much bigger challenge.

There are only so many people at his level, and major fragrance houses have very little bandwidth for smaller, independent brands like mine. Any time someone like Frank spends working on Contrapposto is time he isn’t spending on a major client like Calvin Klein or L’Oréal.

Frank is a genius who is well-known for his woody, spicy scents, so I wanted to challenge him to create a floral. I think I was able to entice him by giving him full creative freedom from the start. I told him to create without budget constraints and see how he could bring his signature DNA into a more traditionally floral fragrance, which ended up becoming Melting Flowers, the first fragrance we finished in the line.

I think trends are really fun, and I love following them. I’m obsessed with TikTok trends, beauty trends, all of it. But I think longevity always comes down to having the best product. If you have the best product, you’ll keep a consumer. Loyalty is made with product, not with brand.

We’ve seen plenty of examples of brands that have spiked and then fallen out of favor because a new, fun, shiny thing comes along. With some products, like Nécessaire’s body wash, I think they create an enormous amount of loyalty because nothing beats it. I still buy it with my own money because I just think it’s the best.

I believe in creating things that are a pleasure to use, so you enjoy the process. They should have some sort of immediate benefit, whether it’s an immediate glow from oxygenation, a cap that clicks in an oddly satisfying way, or the experience of feeling and smelling a product—how it makes your shower smell or how it makes your sweaters smell. Those are the things that keep someone coming back and, I think, make a product timeless.

#6710. Everything to Know About the 2027 Met Gala: Theme, Hosts and More

As ever, the next Met Gala will celebrate the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s spring exhibition. The theme this time? “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday,” examining extraordinary transformations of ordinary garments and materials.

Here’s everything else you need to know about the 2027 Met Gala.

The Met Gala, which provides the Costume Institute’s primary source of funding for all activities, will take place on the first Monday in May: May 3, 2027. The exhibition, which opens to the public on May 9, will be on view through January 9, 2028

Organized by Andrew Bolton, with assistance from Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben, “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will approach its subject in two ways: both by looking at how designers have elevated and experimented with simple garments like tees and jeans, and by considering how humble materials like paper, plastic, and metal have been transformed by fashion. “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will be sponsored by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler, and additional support from Condé Nast and Jordan Roth.

The exhibition replaces the John Galliano study originally planned for 2027.

Inaugurating the Met’s new, nearly 12,000-square-foot Condé M. Nast Galleries, the spring 2026 show, “Costume Art,” considers depictions of the dressed body from across the Met’s curatorial departments, pairing garments with art objects spanning some 5,000 years.

Objects in “Costume Art” are divided into a “series of thematic body types,” ranging from the “Naked Body” and the “Classical Body”—both of which are well represented within the museum’s collection—to those, like the “Pregnant Body” and the “Aging Body,” that have more often been overlooked. It remains on view at the Met through January 10, 2027.

Beyoncé, Nicole Kidman, Venus Williams, and Anna Wintour co-chaired the 2026 Met Gala.

Continuing a tradition from years past, the 2026 Met Gala also had a host committee. That group included committee co-chairs Anthony Vaccarello and Zoë Kravitz, along with members Adut Akech, Angela Bassett, Sinéad Burke, Sabrina Carpenter, Doja Cat, Gwendoline Christie, Misty Copeland, Alex Consani, Elizabeth Debicki, Lena Dunham, Paloma Elsesser, Rebecca Hall, LISA, Chloe Malle, Aimee Mullins, Amy Sherald, Tschabalala Self, Sam Smith, Teyana Taylor, Anna Weyant, Lauren Wasser, A’ja Wilson, Chase Sui Wonders, and Yseult. Additionally, as the lead sponsors for the 2026 gala and exhibition, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos served as honorary chairs.

The 2026 Met Gala livestream was hosted exclusively by Vogue and broadcast live across its digital platforms, including on YouTube and TikTok. To rewatch it on vogue.com, you can head to this page.

That’s kept mostly under wraps; guests must abide by a no-phone (and, therefore, no social media) policy once they’ve entered the museum. But the run-of-show involves cocktails, dinner, and a high-profile performer—or two. (In 2026, that was Sabrina Carpenter and Stevie Nicks.) Attendees always have a moment to explore the exhibition, too.

Decor is, of course, always taken seriously. For 2026, event designer Raúl Àvila was inspired by the design of Northern Italian gardens, with fruit-forward tablescapes (pomegranates, pears, black wine grapes, artichokes, kumquats) set on striped tablecloths. Check back on what was on the menu for this year’s guests, too.

The Met Gala takes place at The Metropolitan Museum of Art each year. Guests from out of town (and even some based in the city) typically stay at hotels nearby, congregating at a few celebrity-favorite spots. The Mark Hotel is always a prime location for star-spotting; in 2026, the likes of Alysa Liu, Alex Consani, Hudson Williams, Lisa, and Odessa A’zion prepared for their big night out there.

The event usually hosts between 450 and 600 attendees, welcoming stars, young creatives, and paragons from the worlds of fashion, the arts, sports, and politics. Here, revisit some of the best looks from frequent guests Blake Lively, Sarah Jessica Parker, Rihanna—and even more of the most memorable Met Gala fashions of all time. Also check out everything that goes into the Met Gala seating chart.

2026 saw a clutch of Met Gala debuts, too: Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, Chase Infiniti, Paul Anthony Kelly, and Sombr included.

There’s always more. Revisit the best looks from the last decade of Met Galas..

#6708. Bob Dylan Dressed Like Timothée Chalamet to Meet the Pope

Today, millions of Americans awoke to social media feeds awash with images of and commentary about a landmark event that seemed nigh-impossible a mere 24 hours earlier. I speak, of course, of this image:

As the nation began to digest the results of a historic election that seemed to herald the arrival of a new America, two of our very best Americans met for a private audience on the other side of the Atlantic: Bob Dylan, the Great American artist, and Pope Leo XIV, the first American Pope. Dylan is in the midst of yet another lengthy European tour—his strongest in some number of years, judging by recent bootleg tapes. On November 2, he played a show at Milan’s Unipol Dome, then jetted over to Rome ahead of a November 5 performance at the ​​Palazzo dello Sport. What better way to kill an off-day than a quick chat with the Vicar of Christ?

It wasn’t the first time Bob met a Pope, as some pointed out. In 1997, he performed for John Paul II at the World Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, donning a dapper Western suit and a fine Stetson for the occasion. He and JP2 made for a bit of an odd couple, the mysterious American gunslinger and the seemingly-nonplussed Polish holy man.

Dylan has somewhat more in common with Pope Leo, a.k.a Robert Francis Prevost, a fellow Midwesterner. But even if the two men hail from similar geography, the sight of them together under the bright fluorescent lights of an anonymous Vatican office looked like the product of a well-crafted AI prompt, if not an outright fever dream. The images were so unexpected, so uncanny, I would’ve been convinced they were fake had they not been published by an official press organ of the Vatican.

Much of the whiplash stemmed from the two men’s appearances. Angel and devil. Spy versus spy. The man in the long black coat and the man in the short white mozzetta. The one liners wrote themselves.

On Wednesday, the Pope wore a clean white cassock and a tidy little zucchetto, with an iron cross hanging down around his neck. In short, he looked like the Pope. I suppose I would say the same about Bob: that he looked like himself. As any good Dylan fan knows, however, the meaning of that phrase has changed radically over the years. Bob’s shifting appearance is almost as notorious as his shifting artistic sensibility. Dust bowl refugee, sharp-suited mod, bohemian poltergeist, whatever this is—the man has worn many hats.

A hoodied Timothée Chalamet, seen with Kylie Jenner, in New York City.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Dylan took a liking to the humble hoodie, a stylistic evolution that intersected neatly with his booze-fueled artistic nadir. The hoodie allowed him to hide in plain sight, even as he continued to take the stage around the world on his Never Ending Tour. It was practical, yes, but it was also a defense mechanism, a way to synthesize his compulsion to perform and his aversion to being seen. That it often looked hard as hell did not hurt. (It should come as little surprise that Timothée Chalamet, who may as well have been born wearing a hoodie, seemed to riff on this era when he was channeling Bob all those months ago.)

In the 21st century, Bob came unstuck from time. On landmark records like “Love And Theft” and Modern Times, Dylan burrowed into an imaginary musical past situated somewhere between the Civil War and the Great Depression. His style shifted to match. In the early aughts, he adopted a full country-western guise, complete with a Lee Van Cleef mustache. In the years that followed, his sartorial inspirations shifted east: a little less cowboy, a little more riverboat gambler, often performing in wide-brimmed hats, long frock coats, and string ties. “Rock and roll Mark Twain” wouldn’t have been an inaccurate descriptor.

Which brings us back to today’s meeting with Pope Leo. On first glance, Dylan’s ensemble is bonkers: western black blouson with contrast stitching along the chest and collar; beneath that, a heavyweight black hoodie zipped to the chest; beneath that, a white collared shirt with several buttons undone, collar loosely drawn together with a polka-dot cravat. The hood is decidedly up, stationed atop a black flat brim cap. In some shots, Bob can even be seen sporting leather gloves and an old-fashioned umbrella, which seems to double as a cane.

Part “Man in Black” sobriety, part rock star debauchery, with a dash of the hypebeast flavor from Timmy’s A Complete Unknown press tour—the man got a damn fit off in Vatican City. There’s no other way to describe it. (It’s a shame Pope Leo left his Rhude jacket back at the Papal Palace.)

Still, it’s a look with roots in Bob’s past, or pasts: the hoodies of the ’90s, the Westernwear of the 2000s, even the polka dots of 1965. No one but Bob would ever dare to pair all these disparate elements, particularly for a private audience with the Bishop of Rome. No one but Bob could.

Someone should come up with a word for that.

#6706. Pierpaolo Piccioli Departs Balenciaga After 1 Year

The designer joined the house in 2025 after 25 years at Valentino.

Pierpaolo Piccioli is leaving Balenciaga after just one year at the helm. The news, announced today by parent company Kering, brings his brief tenure at the house to a close.

“Pierpaolo is an exceptional couturier and creative talent for whom we have the greatest respect,” Kering CEO Luca de Meo said in a statement. “Our ambition is to build on Balenciaga’s avant-garde spirit, honor its remarkable heritage, and continue to push creative boundaries, further establishing the house as a powerful and relevant voice.”

Piccioli joined Balenciaga in July 2025 after a transformative 25-year tenure at Valentino. The designer succeeded Demna, who oversaw a complete rejiggering of the brand’s house codes. Piccioli’s vision for the Spanish house focused less on the streetwear-inflected aesthetic that Demna championed, and more on a romantic, craft-minded approach. As he had at Valentino, the designer bridged the past and present to imagine something softer and more personal for the house.

His debut couture offering in July imbued archival references like the sack dress and the chou wrap with his signature approach to color. He also oversaw buzzy projects, including A New York Minute, a Celine Song-directed campaign starring Sarah Pidgeon, and collaborations with Euphoria creator Sam Levinson and Manolo Blahnik.

“We are deeply grateful for Pierpaolo’s contribution to Balenciaga,” Balenciaga CEO Gianfranco Gianangeli said. “Through his vision, he reaffirmed the couture origins of the house, bringing his considered approach to craftsmanship, construction, and creativity. I would like to sincerely thank him for his dedication, generosity, and collaboration.”

Piccioli’s final Balenciaga collection, which mixed couture techniques with everyday silhouettes, took its bow at Paris Fashion Week in early October. What’s next for the designer is still a question mark, and Kering has yet to name his successor.

#6705. Tapestry Revenues Hit 12% Growth Despite Kate Spade Dip

Tapestry attributed its 12% sales increase to continued momentum from its core Coach consumer, Gen Z — of the 2.6 million new customers welcomed by the brand in Q1, 35% were from the cohort. Coach’s strong performance, however, was offset by a continued decline at Kate Spade.

The company updated its full-year guidance for fiscal 2027 to revenues of $8.5-8.6 billion, an improvement on the previous forecast of $8.4-8.5 billion. “Our first quarter marked a powerful start to the year, with revenue, margin, and earnings growth ahead of expectations,” said CEO Joanne Crevoiserat on Thursday’s call. “We delivered broad-based growth across regions, gaining share and expanding the market.”

Coach sales climbed 16% this quarter, generating revenues of $1.66 billion. Meanwhile, Kate Spade’s fell 10% to $223 million, as the business continues to streamline the brand’s operations, closing unproductive stores, reducing promotions and investing in marketing to build brand relevance — evidenced by Kate Spade’s Fall/Winter 2026 campaign featuring brand ambassador Tyla. The brand also intends to capitalize on its new executive creative director, Jonathan Saunders, who assumed post in August.

“What we need to see is higher customer acquisition [at Kate Spade] to drive long-term growth,” said Crevoiserat. “We’re building our handbag assortment with that in mind.” In the quarter, handbags drove 500,000 new customers to the brand.

Across Coach and Kate Spade, the core leather goods category fueled growth, attracting consumers through accessible pricing. At Coach, handbag AUR — the average selling price of an item over a period — increased by a low double-digit percentage; a focus on bags ranging between $200-$500 will continue. Footwear also supported growth, up more than 20% in the quarter thanks to demand for Coach’s Margot pump, as well as traction in sneakers.

By region, Greater China led the way, with revenues up 39% in Q1. “Other Asia” — including Australia, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, and other countries mostly in Asia — followed at 23%, with Europe close behind at 22%. “Other” — representing mostly royalties earned from licensing and sales in the Middle East — was up 11%, followed by North America and Japan, both up 4%.

For Coach CEO Todd Kahn, Japan’s return to growth was a compelling example that the brand’s strategy had paid off. “We worked hard the last year and a half to reset that market and focus on a younger consumer and relevant marketing,” he said. “It worked, and that’s what gives us confidence that we can continue to replicate this strategy over and over again across the world.”

Kahn added that Coach’s North America revenues continue to grow, while Gen Z remains a core focus for Coach — and Kate Space. “When we win with Gen Z, we tend to win with every other cohort as well,” said Kahn.

#6704. Anne Hathaway and J.Lo Both Love Chocolate Cherry Nails: Here’s How to Wear Them This Fall

The chocolate-brown-meets-cherry-red combo is entirely irresistible.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

At this point, I know all too well that my fall manicure rotation will always include some variation of burgundy nails, chocolate brown nails, and black cherry nails. But what happens when you combine all three? You get chocolate cherry nails, the rich, red-meets-brown manicure that’s been getting a lot of love from Hollywood. Jennifer Lopez has given the moody shade her stamp of approval and Anne Hathaway stepped out wearing a similar cherry cocoa manicure earlier this year.

“Chocolate cherry is one of those wonderfully safe, sophisticated colors that simply goes with everything,” says nail artist Max Estrada. “It’s versatile enough to complement almost any wardrobe, which is precisely why I think celebrities gravitate towards it. It’s glamorous without demanding too much attention, but it certainly knows how to make an entrance.” From short, glossy nails à la Anne Hathaway to longer, dramatic tips inspired by J.Lo, chocolate cherry is proof that sometimes the coolest manicure trends are the simplest ones. Ahead, everything you need to know about getting the look, plus inspiration for your next nail appointment.

Chocolate cherry is the marriage of two fall nail colors: deep cherry red and chocolate brown. Unlike a traditional burgundy, which is more of a winey purple, chocolate cherry is a warmer with a brown undertone. (And it’s pretty dang expensive-looking, I might add.) “It’s incredibly easy to wear without being boring,” says Estrada. “You get the classic elegance of a red manicure mixed with the richness of chocolate brown, creating something that feels expensive, polished and a little mysterious.”

The color is also a perfect transitional shade for fall and winter manicures. As the weather cools off, “we naturally move away from the bright, playful colors of summer towards deeper, warmer tones,” says Estrada. “Chocolate cherry captures that transition perfectly. It has the romance of a deep red and the warmth of autumnal brown, making it an incredibly flattering seasonal color.”

The color looks gorgeous as a simple, solid-color manicure, but there’s also plenty of room to play around with different nail shapes, finishes, and designs. “Personally, I adore a beautifully tapered, long almond nail in chocolate cherry,” says Estrada. “There’s something incredibly vampy, sensual, and sophisticated about that silhouette, especially with an ultra-glossy finish.” He also likes the color with a square nail too.

If you want to get into some nail art, you can go simple or get adventurous with it: “I would also love chocolate cherry with a magnetic velvet cat-eye effect, creating that gorgeous multidimensional movement in the color,” Estrada says. “Or imagine a deep chocolate base with an exaggerated cherry-red French tip.”

Nail prep is always key to a professional-looking mani, especially when you’re working with darker polish, which can be less forgiving. If you’re doing a DIY manicure and you don’t know where to start, here are some tips from Estrada. First, push back your cuticles. “I always recommend gently pushing back the cuticle area, carefully removing excess dead cuticle tissue, refining the nail shape and ensuring every nail looks consistent,” he says.

Next, before applying polish, make sure your nails are clean and dry. “The nail plate should be properly cleansed and prepared before application, while the surrounding skin should be kept beautifully conditioned,” he adds. “Proper preparation means better adhesion, longer wear and a much more luxurious-looking manicure.”

Next, an insider tip: “One of my favorite professional techniques is leaving the tiniest clean margin between the polish and the surrounding skin,” he says. This way your polish is less likely to bleed onto the edges of your finger, which can look messy.

After you’ve applied the polish, he recommends finishing with a cuticle oil for hydration.

#6702. Matt Damon on the Oscars, Tarantino, and the Roles That Got Away

In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollywood, and specifically on a year that will go down as one of that career’s most challenging and rewarding passages.

Damon set 2026 off with The Rip, a throwback pulp thriller that reteamed him with his lifetime BFF Ben Affleck. He then went on to dominate the summer to a degree most actors crossing the other side of 55 wouldn’t dream of, with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey—a noisy, thrilling, engrossing feat of big-budget moviemaking that wouldn’t have worked without an Odysseus compelling enough to command audiences to take the 20-year journey with him. The role demanded everything in Damon’s toolbox, and then some, but the result was a cultural and commercial run that only Spider-Man himself could top.

Jacket (sold as suit) by Norton & Sons. Shirt by Dolce & Gabbana. Pants by Celine. Cummerbund by Charvet. Pocket square by Budd Shirtmakers. Boots by Tom Ford.

This is rare air, and Damon knows it. Lightning struck once for him, with Good Will Hunting in 1997—he never thought he’d see that happen again, much less 29 years later. If exhaustion is the price of beating those odds, then so be it. Still readjusting to life on dry land, Damon sat down to unpack the most unlikely filmmaking experience of his career—and begin working out where he might want to go next.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Matt Damon: That is amazing coming from him. Yes, I did hear about it.

Yeah, I think if you talk to any actor my age, any of the usual suspects, they’d probably say the same thing. I think the more you do it, if you’re working with really good people, you’re always improving, you’re getting better. And then you’re living more life and you have your family dynamics, all of your primary relationships kind of fill up your reservoir. I’ve talked to other actors my age about it, Ben included—I think there’s a tendency to push when you’re younger, a little bit, to try to work yourself up, and the older you get, the more available a lot of this stuff is. These very, very, very big emotions are kind of just sitting [near the surface]. And so you can really relax into the work, and it can be very full without being forced.

I think so, yeah. I mean, I’ve never been a part of a movie like The Odyssey that was…. Well, I guess Oppenheimer, to an extent, was somewhat of a phenomenon as well.

My workload was a lot heavier on this one, and everybody’s was, and that was kind of the joy of it. We knew we were the first ones to ever try to do a full film in IMAX [70 mm], and that comes with a whole host of challenges for every single department. We were all, I think, very patient with each other because we knew what was being asked of the other people. So in terms of the acting department—the IMAX load is two and a half minutes or three minutes. And so these big, heavy emotional scenes—you couldn’t play them all the way through. You’d have to cut them up. And the crew was just awesome, very patient with us. It felt like we were explorers, in a way. We got to be the first ones to do it, and that really bonded us.

I never would have expected it. And also, to play a role that’s so physical and, at my age, to even have a role that’s available on a scale like this. I’d always wanted to make a David Lean movie. To have it come at this point in my life, I felt incredibly lucky, not only to be able to do it, but also to be able to contextualize it. I don’t think I would’ve appreciated it as much 20 years ago.

No, I just don’t think I would’ve been able to understand and to hold as much gratitude as I am and as I did throughout the process. It’s all about how you look at things. And in retrospect, yeah, we were probably cold and wet. There was a lot of physical discomfort that was temporary. But because I felt so grateful to be there, I was just so excited. I was just so joyful the whole time that I didn’t really notice any of that.

[Laughs] There are no sure things, man. I think that’s where you get into trouble, being like, Well, this is a surefire hit. I’ve heard that before.

I felt it when I saw it. There is that thing that can happen where you make a movie, and you feel like it’s really good, and it just doesn’t connect, and there’s just nothing you can do about that. But as the audience reactions started to come in and the critical reactions were great as well, it was like, Okay….

Chris [Nolan], the most nervous he is in the entire process, from the very beginning to the very end, is the eve of the film coming out. He’s genuinely nervous. He talks openly about it, because that is the moment that you put it out into the world and you have to live with the reaction. Ultimately, the audience decides. Once it opened and the responses were what they were, I think I felt like, We’re going to be okay. It was a big bet in the sense that it was a big budget. I’m not used to playing in that arena. The numbers that movies have to get to just to break even at that level are just so beyond the movies that I’m known for.

A few of them. But The Martian, which I think is the biggest movie that I’ve ever headlined—I think The Odyssey made three times what that made. And that was a real hit for me. But there’s this other league of these kinds of movies that are in the billions that I’ve just never….

Well, the thing about a role like that is every single day I was paired with an unbelievable scene partner. One day I’d be working with Annie [Hathaway], and then the next day I’d be working with Himesh [Patel]. It’s following this character through all these different stages of his life and people who are close to him. So every day was a different, exciting little challenge, a little puzzle to figure out. I’ve always said that when you’re working with a great actor, they’re so good that they’re good enough for both of you. And it’s almost like this wave comes and you just stand up on your board and ride it. Then you have Samantha Morton, who literally just picks you up and shoulder-carries you.

It’s very hard to come in and do really intense things in a very short time frame. [Morton’s scenes]—that was under a week of shooting. Each day being incredibly intense. And that was what was so incredible about these actors who would come in. They’re under a lot of pressure. Nobody says that, but we all know the deal. These are critical scenes, and everybody just came in and killed it. It just got more and more exciting as we were going.

I agree. She’s incredible. She’s always been incredible. We had a near-miss working together in 2003—and I got to know her then—in a movie with Heath Ledger. I just think the world of her as an actress, and I was excited when we did the scene. I was like, This one’s going to really work. And I hope—it doesn’t always happen right away, but hopefully it’s lodged her back in the minds of people who are making those decisions, because she’s just extraordinary.

That’s the emotional spine of the movie. A lot of that monologue that I have at the end is in voiceover, but I wrote it all out and I had it on my phone and I would just carry it with me off set. I would just revisit it and run through it a few times, and I was doing that for months and months. Firstly, I thought it was just so beautifully written, but also because I knew that scene had to land. If that lands, then the movie works.

And that also means setting them up as a young couple before he leaves. There’s a lot of engineering that goes into getting to a scene like that and then you have to execute it. I spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about that one.

Well, at that point, the audience has been on the journey with you, and it’s been a hell of a journey, so you don’t have to tell them that. We were tired. That scene I shot with Samantha, oddly, we had come from Iceland, but we were shooting nights, and we came to Scotland, and I had it happen two or three times on this movie where I just didn’t sleep. I was tired and I went to bed, and I’m sure everyone’s had that feeling where you’ve got to get up the next day and you have something that you have to do and you can’t fall asleep and you’re kicking the blanket around and you’re staring at the ceiling. By the time I got to work to do the scene with Sam, I hadn’t slept in 24 hours, and by the end of the day it was 36 or whatever. I remember thinking the great thing about this character is he probably didn’t sleep last night. Don’t worry about it. So the weariness was very real for a lot of the movie.

And I realized in that moment I hadn’t even considered that that could happen. There was a funny thing that happened on The Odyssey. We were in Scotland. I was with my kids. Who knows? I have no right to expect it, let’s put it that way. I don’t want to sound like a broken record, but I have such gratitude for the fact that this came along my path at this point. We got to honor those boys and keep working together if we can. ✦

#6701. Kendall Jenner Reveals the $35 K-Beauty Gua Sha Cream She Uses to De-Puff, Sculpt, and Define

It’s sold out in store, but here’s where to shop it online.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In a skin care space so saturated, it’s refreshing to see a brand get something so right. The product in question? Anua’s Collagen + Retinol Refining Cream. The K-beauty cream has been around since March, but with such burgeoning popularity, it’s been near-impossible to track down.

So why the sudden popularity, and why now? This isn’t just a product that’s risen to fame through celebrity influence. Kendall Jenner (who is a brand ambassador) recently posted a TikTok demonstrating how she uses the sculpting tool as a “post-working detox.” It’s sold out on multiple occasions, proving that its popularity goes beyond a Jenner approval—it’s a brilliant, budget-friendly product that delivers.

This cream is more than just innovative packaging. Beyond the gua sha-style applicator, it cocktails the ultimate trifecta of ingredients designed to smooth, firm, and boost the skin’s elasticity: retinol, collagen, and peptides.

Let’s break that down, starting with retinol: the gold standard for tightening and minimizing fine lines. It uses encapsulated retinol, which, while that may sound like technical jargon, is what makes it so effective and gentle to use. Essentially, it wraps the vitamin A molecule inside a protective polymer to ensure a slow and safe delivery to the deeper layers of your skin. This way, it’s less likely to cause surface-level irritation.

Moving on to collagen. A collagen-pumped moisturizer or mask is not hard to come by. But, despite what the bottle may tell you, even the most expensive players won’t miraculously boost your collagen levels—nor will this cream. The molecule is just too large to be used in topical skin care, so, in this instance, the inclusion of collagen—as well as plumping peptides—is simply used for hydration purposes. They also contribute to the sensorial experience of the cream: it’s rich yet never greasy, lending the perfect amount of lightweight slip to glide the tool over your skin.

The K-beauty skin care scene has always managed to one-up us, whether that’s through innovative formulas or smart packaging—and in this case, both. Cleverly, the cream allows you to combine the sculpting benefits of a gua sha with your moisturizing routine.

The metal, W-shaped tool is designed to seamlessly glide over your skin while slowly dispensing the cream as it goes. In upward strokes, simultaneously squeeze and slide the tool over the contours of your face. Work upwards from the base of your neck, then move on to your jawline, cheekbones, and up to your temples. Repeat this motion three to five times before moving on to the next area.

Move the tool up and down your neck to soothe “tech neck” (stiffness in the neck from too much time looking down at your phone—a sadly relatable truth for us all). But for the rest of your face, the trick is to always glide in an upward motion to gently de-puff and help ease redness.

As with any retinoid, start slow by introducing the cream into your routine three times a week—and temporarily pause any other actives until your skin adjusts to the ingredient. It is cushioned by the peptides, but it’s always good to ease into actives. And, of course, always use an SPF in the mornings.

So while it may not deliver the same sculpting results as seen through a professional lymphatic drainage facial, this is a great alternative to temporarily decrease puffiness until your next appointment calls.

#6700. Ralph Lauren Revenues Climb 10% in Q2, Beating Expectations

“In a consumer landscape often shaped by ever-changing trends, the clarity of Ralph Lauren’s values and timeless style continues to set us apart. We stay true to who we are, and we have a proven ability to evolve with today’s consumer,” president and CEO Patrice Louvet told investors on Thursday. “This is a powerful competitive advantage, and it is translating into sustained momentum and a resilient core consumer with significant opportunities ahead.”

Louvet noted Ralph Lauren’s investment in its brand, products, and lifestyle experiences, highlighting its Wimbledon and US Open activities as standouts in Q2. “These activations are driving strong sustainable growth in new customer acquisition and retention,” he said.

By region, Asia led growth for the quarter. China sales remained strong, Louvet told investors, increasing more than 35%, while Japan and Korea were also up double digits, which he credited to continued investment in localized brand activations and experiences. (The brand recently hosted PoloFest in Tokyo, though the impact of this will be seen in Q3.)

Louvet attributed Europe’s slower growth (up 3% vs 5% in Q1) to the prior year’s strong comparison base, coupled with industry headwinds. CFO Justin Picicci also flagged weaker store traffic in key European markets. North America’s growth beat expectations. “I would argue that we’re actually in the very early innings of our elevation journey in North America, with significant growth opportunities across the region, particularly in the West Coast” Louvet added.

The full-year outlook raise is a result of the quarter’s better-than-expected results, while this morning’s shares decline was down the company’s lowered Q3 projections. “We continue to expect first-half [2027] growth to be stronger than second-half growth, reflecting the timing of this year’s marketing activations and other investments, the timing of planned wholesale shipment shifts and strategic off-price reductions, and more challenging year-over-year comparisons in certain of our key markets,” Picicci said on Thursday’s call.

“As we turn to holidays, we will continue inviting consumers to step into the cinematic worlds that Ralph created with timeless high-quality products and a compelling value proposition,” Louvet said, noting that last year’s trending ‘Ralph Lauren Christmas’ is already back for 2027. “Ralph Lauren Christmas is trending again this year, emerging organically as consumers celebrate and share their love for Ralph Lauren’s iconic products, particularly the bear product in our home collection.”

#6699. My Holiday Wish List Includes One Brand Only

It’s that time of year—when I start dropping not-so-subtle hints to my family and friends about what I want for the holidays. This season, there’s only one thing on my radar—and it comes in a little white box.

Some people think fashion editors are difficult to shop for, because we have extremely singular tastes. While it sometimes rings true that I can be a little particular, there is one fail-safe holiday gift I’m always happy to receive: Pandora jewelry. A charm, a bracelet, a ring, or a chain—personally, I’m open to any, and all, of the above (just in case anyone was wondering).

The holiday wish list practically writes itself, but to give my nearest and dearest a helping hand, I’ve spelled out exactly what each of them could give me below.

We both know I have exquisite taste in jewelry. What can I say? I inherited it from you. With this stackable diamond ring, I’ll carry that fact with me through all of life’s biggest moments. And with any luck, I’ll finally stop stealing from your jewelry box.

Consider this your reminder that Mom isn’t the only woman in your life who delights in a nice piece of jewelry. This Cuban Chain Necklace is as “Timeless” as you are—and as pretty as I am. It’s the perfect Christmas gift for a father to give his daughter.

You make every holiday more special, and when we’re together, that’s the only gift I need. That being said, I wouldn’t refuse a sparkly little memento commemorating our time together. Buy me something nice and I promise I’ll wear it for our next date night.

When I look back on the most magical holidays of my life, I don’t think of the gifts I opened or the food I ate. I think of you, and the joy on your face as you opened the present I chose for you. The best part of my Christmas is always being your Santa.

Remember when we were in elementary school, wearing our matching BFF necklaces? All these years later, our taste in jewelry has evolved, but one thing remains the same: our love for each other. Let’s upgrade the nostalgic symbol with diamonds this time.

#6697. Darian Mensah Might Be the Richest Player in College Football. But He’s Still Going to Class

A decade ago, an interview with the quarterback of the unbeaten, top-ranked team in college football might have involved the player, the reporter, and the team’s sports information director. Maybe the player’s dad stood nearby, keeping guard. But when I talked to Darian Mensah on the Sunday before Halloween, there were five other people on the call, plus a few more sitting in the room with the Miami Hurricanes’ smooth but press-shy signal-caller.

Mensah is the most modern sort of college star, a two-time transfer now at his third school who has navigated a bevy of NIL deals. “I’ve got a great group of people who I think truly want to see me win,” he tells me.

The most notable among them is Malachi Toney, the sophomore receiver who caught 16 balls from Mensah the day before we spoke. By throwing tons of on-target passes, Mensah is comfortably pacing to set college football’s single-season record for completion percentage. As the Canes get ready to travel to South Bend to face No. 4 Notre Dame this weekend, the 21-year-old Heisman Trophy frontrunner is at 80.7 percent, several points clear of second place all-time.

At first glance, Mensah has a simple job: just throw the ball to Toney, who has unparalleled open-field maneuverability. In a 52-point outing against Pittsburgh last month, the two accounted for 194 yards and three way-too-easy scores. “I mean, on the first touchdown, I gave a little signal to Mali,” Mensah recalls. “You can see there's only one guy over the pod of three guys.” The film confirms it: Pitt didn’t put enough defenders near Toney, and Mensah identified it. “You got to keep going to it,” he says.

Mensah loves talking football, though he’s just as happy to get in-depth about how chaotic his life is right now. Mensah is trying to deliver Miami back to its glory days as he manages a variety of commercial arrangements, prepares for his professional future, and, yes, even goes to class, contrary to popular ideas about the NCAA football player experience. “I have to go to class,” he confesses. “Transferring [two] times kind of messed with my credits.” He has three classes per day, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and has had to keep himself eligible at Tulane (which “set the standard for me”), Duke (“probably even a little bit harder”) and now Miami: “Balancing that, school and football, was tough. But I think it set me up for where I'm at now, where maybe it's not as rigorous as far as academics go.”

Mensah gets particularly excited to discuss fashion, which I bring up because most athletes who sit for GQ have at least a moderate enthusiasm for clothes. Mensah, for what it’s worth, is wearing a cropped Adidas T-shirt—the brand is one of his many partners, alongside Dr Pepper and Sling TV. Miami has a roughly $50 million roster, one of the five biggest budgets in the sport. And Mensah, as the team’s star quarterback, is probably its top earner. But I wondered, more specifically, how much money Mensah is set to earn this year between football and his various NIL agreements. “I don’t know,” he demures. “As much as God allows me to.”

Market rate for a Power 4 starting QB is in the low to mid-seven figures, and Mensah is almost certainly on the high end of that spectrum. I’m not interested in pocket-watching, but just a few weeks ago, the United States did pass a bill that would cap how much someone like Mensah can make. The “Protect College Sports Act,” a bill developed by Sen. Ted Cruz and his Democratic counterpart, Maria Cantwell, may come up for a House vote in the upcoming lame-duck session of Congress. (It passed the Senate with a bipartisan array of 77 votes.) The bill would cap school pay to athletes at about $50 million per university, essentially freezing the market right where Miami’s football team currently stands.

The bill’s backers, including seven-time National Champion Nick Saban, have argued that college football player pay is out of control and endangers the integrity of college sports writ large. Essentially, the bill is coming for Mensah’s money, more than practically anyone else among the hundreds of thousands of NCAA athletes. So how does that sit with him?

“I grew up in a single-parent household, and my mom providing for all my siblings was not easy,” he explains. “So to be able to take care of my family in a way that I wasn't able to before has only been a blessing. I don't really know what to say about that other than I'm blessed to be in the position I'm in.”

Mensah doesn’t preoccupy himself with the weight of Miami football's illustrious tradition. He knows the program was “like a dynasty and a powerhouse back then,” and he’s gotten to meet plenty of legends of The U. “Me and the guys always strive to follow in their footsteps,” he says. “But yeah, I was born in 2005...”

In his relatively short life, Mensah has packed in a lot. After playing high school ball in Santa Maria, California, he started his college career as a three-star true freshman at Tulane in 2024. His only other college offer, he told me, was from FCS Idaho State. He entered the transfer portal to play at Duke in 2025, then reentered after winning the ACC Championship last year. In addition to climbing the economic ladder, Mensah has lived in four cities over the past four years. He’s only 21, but he’s got the palette of a washed-up 32-year-old like me. Maple Street Café in New Orleans, which has a chicken lemon dish that is “some of the most amazing pasta I’ve ever had in my life,” is a standout.

Come 2027, there’s a good chance Mensah will make it five cities in five years. He’s eligible for the NFL draft, and should he declare, he’s expected to be taken early in the first round by one of the league’s many QB-needy teams. But I’m a college football guy at heart, so near the end of our call I ask Mensah what he thinks of the impending 24-team playoff format that’s likely to be instituted next season. #6695. Exclusive: The Making of the Costumes of ‘Dune: Part Three’

Somewhere between the paintings of Giotto, the papal courts of medieval Europe, and a mesmerizing photograph of a wealthy woman wearing Dior sunglasses in Iran, Jacqueline West found the visual language for Dune: Part Three. There was Howard Hughes, too, the eccentric American billionaire who spent years living in near-total seclusion in a Las Vegas hotel penthouse, whose lonely existence became a reference for Timothée Chalamet’s burdened Emperor Paul Atreides. And then came Carrie, the 1976 horror film starring Sissy Spacek, which inspired Anya Taylor-Joy’s costumes. For a film set thousands of years in the future, West found herself looking further into the sands of time than ever.

“It’s a gift to get to do all three,” West tells Vogue, reflecting on the nearly eight years she has spent building Denis Villeneuve’s gargantuan sci-fi universe—and surveying a set of images from Dune: Part Three shared exclusively on Vogue. A five-time Oscar nominee whose credits include The Revenant, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, and Martin Scorsese’s Killers of the Flower Moon, West began her career as a fashion designer, running her own label and boutiques in California before making the transition into film. Her meticulous, research-driven approach has since made her one of Hollywood’s most distinctive costume designers.

The trilogy’s final installment, which takes place approximately 20 years after the events of Dune: Part Two, presented West with a new challenge. “It’s a different vision,” she explains. “The script was much more emotional and really character-grounded. Everyone has evolved in very profound ways.”

West and Villeneuve began discussing this new direction while she was in London working on Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger, speaking almost daily before she arrived in Budapest for production. Their three-movie creative partnership is now a well-oiled operation. West begins with the script, followed by long conversations about how Villeneuve imagines each character’s psychological development. From there, she works with her concept artist to develop ideas, bringing sketches and references back to the director.

There has remained an overarching philosophy to the way West dresses the Dune universe. Early in the project, she coined the term “modieval”—a marriage of modern and medieval—to describe the world they wanted to create. Villeneuve, she recalls, was adamant that the designs should remain grounded in reality instead of relying on the conventions of the sci-fi futurist aesthetic. West found her guiding principle in an observation she attributes to Frank Herbert: “to imagine the distant future, look to the ancient past.”

For Part Three, however, even that concept required some reconsideration. “I’ve kept that principle as a flashcard,” she says, “but the story gets darker, and then there’s a redemption. I had to switch from that medieval sense to something almost Renaissance-like. My references got a little more modern in this one.” Her inspirations have expanded to include the paintings of Francisco Goya, the ecclesiastical imagery of the early papacy, Etruscan and North African tribal dress, and the sculptural sartorial language of Cristóbal Balenciaga.

Nowhere is this passage of time more apparent than in Paul Atreides. The young, reluctant messiah of the earlier films has become an all-powerful emperor, haunted by the consequences of his own reign. “With power came enormous guilt,” says West. “He carries the weight of the world on his shoulders.” To communicate this, she turned to the reclusive figure of Howard Hughes, imagining Paul alone at the summit of the Citadel of Arrakis just as Hughes once isolated himself in a Las Vegas hotel suite. West translated that psychological heaviness into robes constructed from substantial fabrics, rich leather, and embroidery.

For Zendaya’s Chani, the approach was almost the opposite. “She’s the moral compass of the story. She’s kept all of her wits about her, along with her wardrobe,” West explains. Now an established leader, warrior, and mother, Chani remains connected to her Fremen heritage through the more traditional stillsuit. That continuity makes the development of the film’s other stillsuits more striking. One of the most ambitious technical undertakings of Part Three was a redesign of the desert survival garment, which West and her team have made more body-conscious. The original suits featured extensive external tubing and multiple visible layers, while the new versions have a scuba-diving quality, with molded acrylic components sitting closely against the body.

“One of [Denis’s] notes was he wanted them sleeker than the first stillsuit,” West explains. As described in the book, the suits still needed to facilitate Herbert’s system for collecting and recycling the body’s moisture in the barren desert. Deep research and experimentation with materials and fabrication brought West to a specially developed, rubber-textured coated Lycra that stretches with the body, incorporating molded hard sections directly into the softer fabric. “They’re kind of melted together,” she says. “It’s like one continuous sheath of molded hard pieces and soft pieces for mobility.” The textile was initially developed in Los Angeles before a factory in Budapest was enlisted to reproduce it at the scale required for production. The plastic components were also largely molded in Hungary, with specialist costume-effects makers developing the initial prototypes.

New armies appear with architectural armor and distinctive headgear drawn from ancient Japanese samurai that required specialist engineering to be made weatherproof. Filming in punishing desert temperatures, West’s team developed cooling suits that could circulate cold water through tubing worn close to the actors’ bodies. She had previously faced the reverse problem on The Revenant, when she needed to keep Leonardo DiCaprio warm in temperatures of minus 40 degrees. This time was about keeping the cast cool enough to endure the heat. “You don’t want unhappy actors going to the set, to Denis…” she says.

Amid the technical innovation, West remains devoted to the tactility of natural materials. “I feel that polyester didn’t make it to the future,” she jokes. “It all melted in the heatwave!” Among her longtime collaborators is a textile artist and designer in Lucca, Italy, who creates many of West’s handwoven textiles, including fabrics for Paul’s robes, from her studio within the medieval city walls. This melding of ultra-modern fabrication and centuries-old craft compounds West’s broader vision for costuming Dune, creating futuristic objects that appear to have lived entire histories.

Princess Irulan’s wardrobe articulates the melancholy of an imperial queen trapped in a deeply unhappy marriage. “I tried to make her Lady Sings the Blues,” the designer says of the predominantly blue palette for Florence Pugh’s character. Irulan’s costumes also continue the ecclesiastical language established for the Bene Gesserit, with elaborate head coverings. West commissioned London-based designer Liria Pristine to create intricate knitted and hand-crocheted metal headdresses, with details that speak to both religious habits and armory. A note in the script that came from the original book described Irulan wearing a cape of intriguing material: blue whale fur. “I thought, ‘What does blue whale fur look like?’” West says. Unable to leave Budapest, she dispatched her assistant designer to Italy to investigate the country’s fabric manufacturers, in search of something to pass for it. He returned with a luminous, icy blue faux-fur-like textile, with which she quickly fashioned a mock-up and dressed a mannequin for Villeneuve's inspection. “He just loved it,” she recalls. “He couldn’t believe we’d found something like that.” The cape is one of Irulan’s most sumptuous pieces, with an almost liquid surface that contrasts with more austere, monastic silhouettes.

Meanwhile, Anya Taylor-Joy’s Alia Atreides, the younger sister of Paul, has grown into a powerful and sinister presence. Her wardrobe, like Irulan’s, draws on the monasticism of the Bene Gesserit. West looked further to Giotto’s religious paintings in Padua and the elongated silhouettes of the characters. As the leader of a cult, West dressed her predominantly in white, also drawing on Sufi-inspired shapes for more dramatic, dynamic movement. West remembered the image of a wealthy woman in Iran, dressed in a white chador and oversized dark sunglasses. “She looked so beautifully sinister,” says West, who recreated the entire look on a mannequin, glasses included, and kept it in her office as a reference throughout production. While West was working on the film, she received a call from longtime collaborator Jack Fisk, the production designer and Sissy Spacek’s husband. With Spacek on the line too, the concept drawing of Taylor-Joy covered in blood prompted a comparison with Spacek’s performance in Carrie by Spacek herself. “So Carrie automatically became a reference,” West says. “I put more and more and more blood all over Anya Taylor-Joy! When I showed Denis, with all the blood, he said ‘oh, you know she’s worked with Scorsese.”

Robert Pattinson joins the cast as the shapeshifting Scytale, and has a wardrobe that relates that slippery persona, from his stillsuit to his Fremen robes. West initially imagined his look through the imagery of the early papacy—particularly the period when the papal court moved from Rome to Avignon. She was drawn to the historical associations of religious persecution. “I wanted to keep him unsettling and menacing,” she says. Jason Momoa also returns as Hayt, a “ghola” (a genetically engineered replica of his character Duncan Idaho), wearing luxurious-looking garments. “He’s almost presented like a gift to Paul,” says West.

It’s been a deeply personal and emotional piece of work, one she’ll find hard to let go of. “[Denis is] so passionate about this project,” West says. “It was really important to him that we all got it right. We were all very emotionally involved with it.” After nearly eight years and three films together, West likens their creative relationship to an orchestra. “Denis [is] the conductor and we’re all the instruments,” she says, “and he keeps us all in the right key.”

#6693. Our Favorite Loafer Now Comes in Menswear’s Favorite Leather

A store I worked at in the 2010s used to stock dozens of styles of well-known shoe brands, and while our inventory was well-stocked, the rare cordovan loafers that popped up were almost mythical. There would be murmurs of a possible restock and by the time I showed up for my shift they’d be gone. In other words, cordovan loafers aren’t always easy to come by. I bring this up because Meermin’s 25th Anniversary Unlined Penny Loafer is now available in a gorgeous burgundy shell cordovan—one that, considering the nature of both the material and the build, should hold up for another 25 years of consistent wear.

First, a quick little primer on Meermin: the Mallorca-based, family-owned shoemaker started in, you guessed it, 2001. They decided to put decades of luxury industry experience into their own, less-marked-up, dexterously-made products. 25 years later, and the Unlined Penny Loafer is the catalog’s crown jewel—tenaciously timeless, super versatile and as comfortable as loafers come—and thus the bedrock the brand has riffed-upon for the anniversary.

We should also note that shell cordovan leather is very much not like the other leathers. For starters, it can only come from horsehide, and specifically from the underlayers of the rump, which is the (actual) technical term for the ass and also a very finite region of hide. Cordovan is notoriously sturdy. Like, damn-near-indestructible, will-outlive-the-cockroaches, kind of durable. And, like many long-lasting materials, it develops an inimitable character with age, such that one could argue it gets more beautiful with each scuff.

And if you’re worried about the bottoms of a pair of shoes designed to last decades—and millions of steps—the flexible chestnut bark-tanned leather outsoles Meermin employs are affixed with a resoleable Goodyear welt, so you won’t need to fret about the inevitably asymmetrical wear-and-tear. If there was a single nit to pick with the endeavor, it’d be that these are a limited release and don’t allow for a whole lot of waffling. So, if you’re in the market for some forever loafers, your search could be over in a matter of minutes. Head on over to Meermin to check ‘em out in all their glory.
