#6660. How Palace Kept Its Cool

It’s rare that almost every member of a company’s upper management team is a diehard skateboarder. But at Palace — the British apparel brand founded in 2009 — it’s par for the course. Gareth Skewis, who co-founded the company with Lev Tanju, cites this as one of the core reasons the international, multi-million-pound business has been able to expand and maintain its credibility in subcultures across the globe.

This week, the brand aired an exclusive capsule with Burberry at its new store on London’s Poland Street — a milestone for a brand that bet on quintessentially British skate style at a time when competitors were largely inspired by North American streetwear. Burberry and Palace had many conversations over the years, discussing projects and the right time to make the collaboration happen, Skewis tells Vogue Business. Then, the right opportunity arrived. “They’ve been amazing. [Burberry creative director] Daniel Lee and his team, and [CEO] Joshua Schulman have been really great to work with.”

The new Palace store opened to the public on Thursday.

Palace spawned from a motley crew of Southbank skaters, who rented a rundown flat in South London, known informally as “The Palace”. Together, they named themselves the Palace Wayward Boys Choir (PWBC), with core members including Tanju and the brand’s head of creative, Stuart Hammond. Tanju and Skewis were in discussion about a brand around the same time Tanju secured a slot on photography and film duo Tim & Barry’s “Don’t Watch That TV” YouTube channel — a precursor to grime’s streaming boom — to air his skate news program, The PWBC Weekly News, every Wednesday at 4.20pm. “The first time I saw any of that, I was like, ‘This is the most interesting thing I’ve seen in skateboarding in 20 years,’” says Skewis, who decided after episode one that Palace would be the brand name.

In 2015, Palace set up shop on Soho’s Brewer street, which thrived — not dissimilar to the likes of Supreme, Gimme 5, and the Hideout — on its cult appeal, staffed by skaters and DJs who naturally communicated the brand’s messaging. During the peak of the late-2010s streetwear boom, the locale was consistently thronged with teens and twenty-somethings who would camp out for hours ahead of big drops. In recent years, whenever I’ve visited the store, it’s been quieter, but still busy.

Gareth Skewis, co-founder of Palace, believes in the power of IRL experiences to channel brand messaging.

Fast forward to now, and the brand is a familiar figure within fashion, luxury, and sportswear, having partnered with the likes of Harrods, Vivienne Westwood, Moschino, and Arc’Teryx, as well as niche labels, such as Japan’s Beams Plus and Evisu.

For the year ended January 31, 2026, the company reported £27.6 million in turnover, down from £34 million the year prior. The filing on Companies House attributed this to product volume discipline and strategic release cadence in line with a focus on long-term positioning over short-term revenue. Before that, the company had reported year-on-year growth amid the post-Covid bounceback. (The brand declined to comment directly on financials.)

“Lev [Tanju, co-founder] and I have the luxury that we’ve never done anything we didn’t want to do,” says Skewis. “Not everybody gets it all the time, and I think that’s a good thing.” Sometimes, that means collaborations or product innovations that are more niche (Palace x artist Dick Jewell), while other times, it’s a simple win. The 10-piece Burberry capsule — launched exclusively in the new Palace London flagship — falls under the latter. “Who doesn’t like [Burberry’s] Camden car coats?” Skewis shrugs. “We’re south of the river, and they’re north of the river, so it’s an interesting juxtaposition,” he adds, observing the city’s internal rivalry.

The limited drop and new store come at a pivotal moment in Palace’s trajectory. Last weekend, the company celebrated its first year partnering with Nike, following the end of its 10-year contract with Adidas, which manifested in a recurring collaboration alongside other ad-hoc partnerships. Nike took the spot in 2025 with the arrival of Manor Place, a Grade-II-listed Flemish revival building housing a skatepark that transforms into a five-a-side soccer pitch through state-of-the-art hydraulics. Architecture studio Jam designed the multifunction venue; it’s also the Palace office.

With Nike, Palace has produced a series of ongoing collaborations, while Manor Place functions as a contemporary “third space”, open to the public for daily use and offering a year free in studio space to resident artists and creatives, a gallery space, and boxing classes. (It’s also hosted London designer incubator Fashion East’s shows since Fall/Winter 2026.)

The skatepark, architecturally inspired by famous skate spots across the British capital, has ostensibly been a major hit. (Anecdotally, my personal visits confirmed consistent footfall.) It also provides Palace with a pipeline for new talent — rappers, skaters, hosts, and photographers — who collaborate with the brand on commercial videos, as well as a consistent flow of cultural happenings to build TikTok and Instagram content around.

The hydraulic five-a-side-pitch-cum-skatepark at Manor Place.

For big brands seeking to capitalize on youth culture, the space is a case study for why giving back and engaging organically matter. “When we first discussed it with Nike, it was really interesting to see how much they got behind it,” recalls Skewis. “And truthfully, anyone who’s living in any inner-city on the planet currently knows that there are not many places young kids can go and do things that are both free and safe.”

Like most office workers, Skewis loves Fridays. “Manor Place opens at about 12pm. Anyone who’s in England will just come and skate,” he says. “You’ve literally got 12-year-old kids skating with people who are either professional skateboarders or who have jobs running ad agencies or in the city.”

For Skewis, physical retail is the best way to communicate a brand’s message, stronger than out-of-home and digital advertising or exclusive brand dinners. “I like standing in spaces where you understand what that brand smells and sounds like, and the way the customer service and staff work with you,” he says. Manor Place, which has a shop, does this — and hopefully the new store will, too.

The new 250-square-meter store — primed with David Sims photography, parquet flooring, and huge screens to play skate videos — opened to VIPs on Wednesday, followed by a public unveiling on Thursday. Alongside Palace’s concession in Dover Street Market London, Poland Street is the brand’s core direct-to-consumer (DTC) location in London.

Inside 8 Poland Street, Palace’s new London flagship.

The two-story space is specced with light wells, stained-glassed windows, bare concrete, museological displays, stone plinths, and a number eight-shaped door handle. (The eight motif also appears in the Burberry collection.) It reflects Palace’s USP as a culturally curious, luxury-adjacent skate brand. “It’s got that tension: certain bits of iconography that don’t feel like they fit in classic skateboarding retail,” Skewis adds.

The designer of the new store, Steve Oh, has worked with Palace for several years, designing the brand’s spaces in South Korea, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Singapore. Indeed, Palace has ramped up its expansion in the Asia-Pacific region, now counting DTC outposts across Japan, South Korea, China and Singapore, as well as its US locations.

But how has the brand carried its hyper-London brand messaging and subcultural capital to foreign climes and consumer landscapes as vastly different as East Asia’s? Through meeting fellow skaters and creatives on the ground. “If you’ve skated for long enough, there are natural scenes,” Skewis says. “We’ve got really close friends in Shanghai, Hong Kong, Seoul, New York.” In fact, Skewis has known Palace’s strategic advisor for the China region, Stéphen Khou, for some 25 years, acquainted through his travels in France and London’s ground zero for skating, Southbank. “It’s really been an organic approach, and I think that’s kind of what Palace is. We’re not trying to be anything that we’re not.”

The roadmap for the next 10 years? Skewis plays it cool. “If we can continue to do things like Manor Place, put out skate videos, do the things we love… That’s really what we’re about.”

#6658. The Fringe Pieces Fashion Insiders Are Wearing This Fall

Runways say this is the adornment of the season.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fringe never really goes out of style. No matter the season, you can always expect to see the embellishment swaying from the arm of a suede jacket or dangling off a leather bag. So when it comes to trends around the design detail, it’s a mere matter of what form the fringe takes. Lately, fashion’s found itself in a fringe fixation, prompting the trim to move beyond the Western-inspired looks it’s best known for.

Fringe re-emerged on the scene last fall when spring/summer 2026 catwalks from Bottega Veneta, Givenchy, and Chanel showcased the adornment as playful ornamentation for skirts, bags, and even shoes. By the fall/winter 2026 season, others were beginning to chime in with their own takes. There were the boho-inspired bags from Etro, the romantic wispy dresses from Ulla Johnson, and restrained silhouettes from Altuzarra.

Whether you’re looking for a bold statement or a little wink of style, fringe remains a simple way to add flair to any outfit. And right now, there’s a fringed version of just about any wardrobe piece you could think of. Between the classic leather staples and newer avant-garde styles, you’ll find something for every style sensibility.

Do an online search for fringe jackets, and you’ll find no shortage of options to shop. Leather and suede remain tried-and-true materials for this style of outerwear—but now there’s also a plethora of other textiles to shop as well. Opt for Toteme’s viral scarf coat if you’re in the market for a new winter coat, or this tweed number from Etro if you’re looking for a polished piece you can wear to the office.

Nili Lotan Eloi Fringe-Trimmed Suede Jacket

Simon Miller Mabel Vegan Leather Fringe Jacket

If recent fall/winter 2026 runways from Givenchy and Proenza Schouler show us anything, it’s that fringe dresses are reaching new heights. The trim is an especially pretty touch to formalwear and event dresses, providing playful movement with every step to even the simplest silhouettes.

Cara Cara Troy Floral-Print Fringe-Trimmed Cotton-Blend Jersey Midi Dress

Ciebon Nella Asymmetric Fringe Midi Dress

Cult Gaia Noosha Fringed Silk Halterneck Maxi Dress

Just like dresses, fringe skirts are experiencing a similarly sophisticated evolution. Lately, the style has favored sleek satin fringe to create a distinct piece that will immediately elevate anything it’s paired with.

Bottega Veneta Fringed Knitted Silk Midi Skirt

Alaïa Tassle Fringed Asymmetric Wool-Gabardine Midi Skirt

Anna Sui Asymmetric Floral-Flock Fringe-Trimmed Crepe Midi Skirt

The sky’s the limit when it comes to fringe bags these days. There’s long fringe and short fringe. There’s standard leather and suede trim that adds a timeless flair, or more dramatic confections made of sequins, beads, or feathers. With beaded tassel bags on the rise, it makes sense that fringe would take similar cues for an eclectic flourish.

Fendi Croissant Fringed Calf Hair Shoulder Bag

Nili Lotan Asher Fringed-Trimmed Suede Shoulder Bag

After Givenchy debuted a pair of bold fringed mules as part of its spring/summer 2026 collection, fringe exploded onto shoes—heels in particular—in a big way. These Boudoir mules, as they came to be known, introduced a playful take on fringe footwear. Now it’s an ultra-luxe, fashion-forward style that’s perfect for those who never shy away from making a statement.

#6656. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6655. Are Young Men the New Kings of the Swing Vote?

Two years ago, it seemed that the young men of Gen Z were shaping up to be hardcore conservatives. More than half of them voted for Donald Trump’s second presidency, refuting the idea that young people tend to lean progressive. Liberal media panicked about finding “a Joe Rogan of the left” who could reach them, and conservatives took a victory lap. “Gen Z Has Turned Right!” Fox News’s Greg Gutfeld announced, citing a report from the Harvard Kennedy School that highlighted, among other insights, the ways social media has led to an increase in conservatism among young folks. A Turning Point USA Poll from around the same time declared Generation Z “the most conservative generation in decades.”

On Tuesday night, though, as a blue tidal wave flipped states from Iowa to Texas, it was young men who comprised a critical segment of the new Democratic coalition. As reported by CIRCLE, a non-partisan research organization at Tufts University, white men between the ages of 18 to 29 voted blue by a 10-point margin; in 2024, exit polling indicated that 56% of all young men voted for Donald Trump. Even more remarkably, young people across the board voted for Democratic congressional candidates by a 40% margin, according to data from NBC.

“In the wake of 2024, there was this whole catastrophizing panic,” says Aidan Kohn-Murphy, the founder of Gen Z for Change (formerly known as TikTok for Biden) and a prominent political influencer. “Oh my God, everything we thought about Gen Z is wrong. It's actually a conservative generation. And no, that's not what was happening. I mean, a huge part of Gen Z just didn't show up to vote because they didn't feel like they had a reason.”

For Democratic strategist Eric Stern, connecting with men on an emotional level was critical in getting them out to vote. Stern has worked on Ruben Gallego and John Fetterman’s campaigns; his political ad agency, FIGHT, has produced spots for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed, and Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa, to name a few. This election cycle, Stern sought to change voters’ perception of what a Democrat can look like.

“Our most notable ad of the general election was Bob [Brooks] standing in front of a literal dumpster fire and then putting it out because he's a firefighter,” he said. Brooks, now the Representative-elect in the Lehigh Valley, flipped his seat on Tuesday. “A ton of Latino men are really into boxing and MMA fighting, and so Ruben [Gallego] held events around boxing,” Stern told me. For Texas’ Hinojosa, who'll become the state’s first Democratic governor in 35 years when she's sworn in in January, that meant running an ad during Mexican boxing champion Canelo Álvarez's match against Christian Mbilli, an event with a massive Latino viewing audience.

Still, Kohn-Murphy and Stern both argued that the main issue on the ballot this cycle was affordability. “If you look at polling, far and away the top issue for voters is cost of living,” Stern said. “And so you can run a million ads saying that ‘Jane Doe is for they/them,’ but it's not going to resonate with people in the same way if they can't afford to keep their lights on.”

When I asked Republican political consultant Kirsten Kukowski about young men voting blue, she brought up affordability too. After all, nearly nine months into the Iran War, a barrel of oil still costs $100. “Men and young men voted with their bank accounts,” she offered. “And for the last several years, that's how they've been voting. And I think that's how Donald Trump won that group two years ago, because he was talking about affordability and inflation.”

Kukowski, the former Communications Director for the Republican National Committee, now runs her own firm, K2 and Company, out of Minneapolis. “At some point here, people expect results,” she continued. “People expected results from Donald Trump, and they didn't see that. So now we're on the clock again for another two years.”

#6654. I’m an American Living in Madrid. This Week, I Felt Closer to Home Than Ever.

It’s when you hear yourself saying things like, “En Nueva York, no somos de Trump” to your workout class—all Spaniards—that you realize how far you are from what’s happening back home.

By “you” I mean “I,” and by “when” I mean on November 3, when I explained to my fellow burpee-ers, mid-class, that my absentee ballot hadn’t arrived in time, but it was okay because I’m not from a swing state. (Even with a better translation than I came up with, “swing state” is a hard concept to parse in a parliamentary democracy.) It’s also when I got my first real taste of an exquisite expatriate loneliness that’s normally held at bay by long lunches, shockingly affordable wine, and universal healthcare—a.k.a. life in Spain.

We moved to Madrid in August 2025. Our move wasn’t an escape; we’d been working on visas and house rentals and school visits since long before the aforementioned’s second term. We moved for a change of pace, to expose our son and ourselves to a different culture, for Spanish immersion. But, as I don’t need to remind you, there was a lot—real or projected—to run away from. USAID had been dismantled. ICE had begun violent, government-sanctioned kidnappings. Our schools were rife with gun violence and vaccine hesitation. Eric Adams was the mayor of New York, Karoline Leavitt ruled the press podium. Remember Pam Bondi? How about Kristi Noem?

We didn’t run away. But we watched the American promise wither from our apartment in the Spanish capital with a mixture of shock, relief, and guilt. Our neighbors in New York were organizing against ICE. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was naturalizing 500,000 undocumented migrants in Spain. I wished to be nowhere but here–where, to my left-leaning sensibility, a kind of deep humanity seemed to prevail in both the social and political spheres.

It’s true that I also missed the magnificent symphony of Zohran Mamdani and the Knicks championship. (And the irony of the privileged nomad placed me in New York when Spain won the World Cup, so I missed that, too.) But neither absence touched the same strange depth in me as waking up hourly the night of November 3 as polls closed on the East Coast, then in the Midwest and on the West Coast, then falling asleep for an odd hour between 5 a.m. and 6 a.m. (GMT +1) and awaking to the blue blue map, to news of the first Black female governor—in Georgia, no less—the first Native American governor, the first Native American female senator, the first openly gay senator, and to Texas. Texas!!!!

I felt…what? I was—I am—overjoyed. I’m more than overjoyed. I have hope. I sense a renewed truth to the American promise, one founded not on the erasure of Native Americans, Black people, and other groups, but on solidarity with them. I also felt a painful disbelonging. I did not help it happen. I did not lay the cornerstones for what we’ve built. I can’t rightfully share in the fullness of the celebration.

I can imagine a disbanding of ICE, a renewal of climate commitments. I let my mind entertain the possibility of our passing meaningful gun control. I do not resent having missed it, exactly. But I am bad at translating how much it all matters to the Spanish women with whom I have daily coffee. And I don’t have language, certainly not in Spanish and perhaps not in English, for the degree to which this election’s rebuke changes how I imagine my child’s future. And then, also, how to describe an unfamiliar sensation that came over me as I made my son’s daily bocadillo de jamon. Maybe no one can say it better than one woman whose wisdom has gone viral.

I don’t live there right now, but my community is where this is happening. For the first time in a very long time, I felt American pride.

#6651. 13 Rugby Shirts Under $150 for Credible Old-Money Cosplay

Historically, rugby shirts are a somewhat conflicted character in the never-ending tale of menswear shirting. On one hand, they’re a prep staple on par with OCBDs, loafers, and boat shoes. On the other hand, they were quite literally designed to handle the rigors of full-contact rugby and were later embraced by folks who proudly call themselves dirtbags.

There’s an interesting duality to rugby shirts: they can feel twee or they can feel traditionally sporty. Thanks to this polarity, it makes it even easier to fit into your wardrobe. Regardless of which camp you fall in, rugby’s crush. And thanks to a recent resurgence, we thought it would be a good idea to highlight some rugby shirts under $150.

Not only are they traditionally as comfortable as any polo you own, they’re also refined enough to take into stuffier settings, rugged enough to handle some serious outdoor exploration and flexible enough to wear from Friday to Monday morning (but don’t do that, probably). And while we love an expensive version of, well, anything, we also love it when we can find some killer alternatives for prices we’d like to think of as reasonable. There wasn’t a paucity of options either, so we rounded up 13 of our favorites, right below.

One of the least expensive options on this list is also one of the best—the loose, shorter cut makes wearing it with jeans, some chinos or virtually anything else in your closet as easy as any polo you have in the arsenal.

J.Crew has a few louder options in the catalog, but the pared-down, solid-bodied iterations are even more affordable and play a supporting role with as much skill and charisma as your favorite character actor.

There is an actual science to color combinations, and Gramicci deserves an Einstein Award for this one.

When done right, a rugby can be one of the best outdoors shirts on the market, and this one is just that: super comfortable, a little hardy and delightfully remiscent of the ones you would've seen in Camp 4.

There's simply no way that the company founded by an original Camp 4 denizen could ever make a rugby not worthy of a Half Dome assault, and it's also improbably still under $150.

Alex Mill makes a few killer monochromatic, garment-dyed variations of this striped number, but this one is more fun than those and we could all use a little bit of fun when the days are as short as they are now.

It's odd to call something a rugby if it doesn't have a contrasting placket, but this one gets a pass because everything else checks out and it's also made out of a hardy-ass jersey fabric.

One of the best rugby shirts we've found also happens to meet the rigorous price qualifications of this list—and now it's half-off—and it's not all that often that the best of anything is also a value play.

Putting "Iconic" in the name is one of those things that can backfire on you if it doesn't live up to the billing, but this one does and remains both a standard of the genre and, against all odds, under $150.

Very few brands appreciate the rugby—or the possibilities that exist under the rugby banner— more than 18 East, and not only is the Harold reimagining the notion of stripe spacing within the genre, but it's also the only short-sleeve option on this list.

This one is going to keep working its way into lists as long as its available because sometimes a brand just nails it. In this case, the cocktail of perfectly-faded brown and black is radiating Leatherheads (complimentary) and the cut is the comfy kind that can layer on either side.

Some big ol' stripes, a woven collar and a cool little oxford cloth hit at the inside of the neck are just a few details elevating this one from "not bad" to "oh hell yeah." (It's also on sale, which always helps.)

Hear me out: I've made a habit of finding stuff in the women's section that fits better than anything on the men's side, and this rugby has all the trademark elements of those past hitters. Also, it might be the softest one on this whole list.

#6650. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6649. Black Doves Season 3: Everything We Know So Far

Warning: Spoilers for Black Doves season 2.

Black Doves is the latest spy thriller gracing our television screens, this time with Keira Knightley stepping into tactical gear. Knightley stars in the Netflix show as Helen Webb, a highly lethal agent in the Black Doves organization responsible for trading government secrets—but things only become more complicated in season 2 when her husband, Wallace, becomes the prime minister of the United Kingdom.

Fans were left on the edge of their seats when Wallace finally asked her who she really is after putting the safety of her family over her devotion to the organization, but will she actually tell him? And will the show receive a third season? Here’s what we know so far.

Netflix has not confirmed if Black Doves will receive a third season. The streaming giant typically waits until the first few weeks after the show’s release to announce if a show has been granted a renewal.

Fans are hopeful that Knightley and Ben Whishaw will return as the show’s central duo, in addition to their fellow recurring cast members Sarah Lancashire (Reed), Kathryn Hunter (Lenny Lines), Ella Lily Hyland (Williams), Gabrielle Creevy (Eleanor), and Agnes O’Casey (Dani). Season 2 saw the arrivals of Ambika Mod (Laila), Babou Ceesay (Mr. Conteh), Sam Riley (Patrick), Sylvia Hoeks (Katia Chernov), Goran Kostic (Alexi Chernov), and Samuel Barnett (Jerry).

There are no plot details for season 3 yet, but the finale gave fans plenty to hope for in a potential next season, due to its many bombshells.

Katia (Hoeks) is revealed to be Vita, the long-lost daughter of Mrs. Reed, the leader of the Black Doves. Believing she was abandoned, she tries to take down the Black Doves organization as a whole and attempts to force Helen to kill Wallace during a standoff, but this plan backfires—agents quickly swoop in and kill her, and in her final moments, she tells Reed that she loves her. As a consequence, Helen kills her family’s nanny, Marie (Chesworth), after finding out she worked alongside Vita to endanger her kids.

Sam leaves Helen and heads back to Italy in the pursuit of a quieter life after settling his debt to Patrick, leaving the status of their platonic relationship unclear. Patrick still poses a threat to the Black Doves organization, and the fight with him will likely continue into a third season if the show is renewed.

Helen also nearly tells Wallace her true identity, but before she can, the credits roll.

Black Doves season 1 premiered on Netflix in December 2024, with season 2 arriving in November 2026. Season 3 could arrive in fall or early winter of 2028 if it follows the same release schedule. We’ll have to wait for official news from Netflix.

#6648. Inside Gabby Thomas and Spencer McManes’s Romantic Rainy-Day Wedding in Cabo

It all started with an Instagram follow. Track and field Olympian Gabby Thomas and Kaviva non-alcoholic beverage brand founder Spencer McManes had mutual friends, but it wasn’t until Gabby followed Spencer back that he made his move. “He slid into my DMs almost instantaneously,” the sprinter and three-time Olympic gold medalist remembers. What began as a direct message soon led to a first date at a speakeasy in downtown Austin, where the two spent three hours talking about everything from pizza to Game of Thrones.

“Looking back, it’s wild to think our story started with a phone notification that could’ve just been a fleeting message,” Gabby says.

Spencer proposed nearly two and a half years later, in March 2025, on an Austin rooftop overlooking the city. “I had planned a staycation for us to celebrate the start of her season, as I had done the previous two years,” Spencer explains. “Gabby’s friends were a huge help getting the flowers and candles set up on the rooftop, and then they hid as I walked her up.”

“I was so surprised,” Gabby remembers. “When I say I did not see it coming, I truly didn’t. Celebrating the start of my track season isn’t out of the ordinary, so it was the perfect cover. Looking back, though, I’ll admit there were clues leading up to it—like my friends’ RAV4s parked outside the Airbnb and someone leaving the front door open to set up the flowers…but I was none the wiser!” Following the proposal, the couple celebrated with an intimate dinner alongside close friends at J. Carver’s, Gabby’s favorite spot in Austin.

A year and a half later, on October 30, the couple exchanged vows at Garza Blanca Resort & Spa in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. “It was important to us that the celebration felt like one big, ongoing party, where our friends and family stayed at the resort together,” Gabby says. “We actually booked the venue before either of us had ever set foot in Cabo—and it all worked out!”

The couple approached wedding planning with an equally easygoing attitude. “I really wanted the process to be a fun, shared experience between the two of us,” Gabby says. “Every decision felt natural and organic. Instead of worrying about what would look good to everyone else, I imagined myself on the day: What would that Gabby really value and appreciate? Since we’re both pretty chill, we hired the wedding-planning team at About Love to help so we could focus on the personal touches that meant something to us.”

“We focused on what made sense for us and what would keep us happy—and relaxed—on the day,” Spencer adds. “We made sure to weave in the things that matter most, from the cities we’ve explored together and our dogs to our family, friends, and, of course, pizza.”

For the festivities, Gabby wore three custom looks by Galia Lahav—one each for the ceremony, reception, and after-party. “I went dress shopping over a year ago in Austin to get a feel for my personal style,” she says. “I was expecting to fall in love with a simple silhouette, but once I put on my Galia Lahav lace basque-waist gown, I knew it was the one. I felt like a princess. It was romantic, elegant, and dramatic. I added sleeves and a veil, which gave it a Victorian-esque vibe.” She accessorized with Maria Elena earrings and Jimmy Choo ballet flats.

Spencer opted for a white tuxedo jacket paired with black trousers. “I wanted to wear white for the occasion because I probably won’t get to wear a snazzy white dinner jacket again,” he says. While his groomsmen wore classic black tuxedos, Spencer introduced an unexpected heirloom element: “I wanted to help my groomsmen stand out from the sea of suits, so I surprised them with bolo ties to wear in place of black bow ties,” he explains. “My great-grandfather passed down his bolo tie to me, and it has become a staple in my wardrobe for weddings and black-tie events. I thought what better way to honor my groomsmen than to give them each a bolo tie for our wedding.”

The bridesmaids wore dresses by Austin-based brand Revelry—a nod to the Texas city the couple calls home. “I spent time with their founder, Michelle, to find a color that felt right,” Gabby says. “We landed on honey beige, which was stunning. The women chose their own silhouettes; it was important to me that while they matched in color, they showed up authentically as themselves. I didn't want rigid rules around how they wore their hair, their jewelry, or even their shoes.”

The ceremony unfolded directly on the sand with the Pacific Ocean as the backdrop. “It had been raining all day,” Gabby recalls. “But right as our ceremony began, the rain cleared, and a vibrant rainbow appeared behind us just as I reached the altar.”

Guests took their seats along the draped aisle under soft, overcast skies that lent an ethereal quality to the setting. “Walking down the aisle escorted by both my mother and father, there were so many emotions,” Gabby says. “The best way to describe it is grateful, excited, and completely anchored in the moment. Having my grandfather officiate made it that much more personal. I spent most of the service gazing into Spencer’s eyes, but I remember pausing to look out at everyone who had traveled to celebrate with us—and just being overwhelmed with love.”

“Gabby completely stole the show,” Spencer says. “We locked eyes for the entire ceremony. It was unforgettable.”

After the vows, the newlyweds stole a quiet moment to take sunset portraits along the water. “It was misty and wet on the beach, but we embraced it,” Gabby says. “We even filmed a few TikToks with the wedding party before sending everyone off to cocktail hour.”

Before making their grand entrance into the reception, Gabby slipped into her second Galia Lahav look—a design she had initially tried on as a ceremony contender and couldn't stop thinking about. “It was flashy, sultry, and unexpected, which was exactly the vibe I wanted for dinner and dancing,” she explains. “I had a bustle added so I could execute our choreographed first dance effortlessly and hit the Dougie all night long.”

The dance floor remained packed from the opening track to the final send-off. “Even though weather forced us to move inside at the last minute, our guests brought incredible energy,” the bride says. “It was a diverse crowd, and the playlist reflected that—a mix of hip-hop, throwback classics, and a little country, but mostly heavy on hip-hop. Everywhere I looked, someone was smiling or dancing. There was truly nothing like it.”

Just before the late-night saxophonist took the stage, Gabby changed into her third and final ensemble: Galia Lahav’s playful, short Hazel dress, paired with custom New Balance sneakers. “It was flirty, fun, and let me dance completely freely,” she says. “I felt like the life of the party.”

Reflecting on the weekend, Gabby adds: “I feel like the luckiest person in the world. Not just because rain is good luck, but because the people in that room made it the best day of our lives. There wasn’t a single second where we weren't smiling, dancing, or celebrating. We’re just so grateful.”

#6645. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6642. Jordan Firstman on Club Slang, Directing His Friends, and the Perfect Date Night

Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut, Club Kid, was the talk of Cannes this year, earning a seven-minute standing ovation and starting a bidding war.  “I had a funny LA tarot card reader right before Cannes. I hadn’t sold the movie until Cannes and she was like, ‘This card is A24, and this card is Neon. If you go with A24, I think there’s a multi-picture deal happening,’” Jordan Firstman shared with Chloe on The Run-Through.

The film is out Friday and features Cara Delevigne, Saturn Risin9, and a cast of extras found on Grindr and in the local nightlife scene. But one of the standouts is newcomer Reggie Absoholm, who plays Arlo, the long-lost 10-year-old son that Peter (played by Jordan) finds out he has. “I do stuff to, like, cringe [Reggie] out ’cause I just like it. I do feel like a dad to him sometimes, and, like, it’s fun. I feel like that’s what made him comfortable on set was just being able to make fun of me.”

In his conversation with Chloe, Jordan shares why he chose to center New Yrok for a story about friendship and club culture, gives her a quick rundown on drug lingo, and talks about being newly in love.

Listen to the full conversation here—and read an abridged version below.

Chloe Malle: Jordan, welcome to the podcast. Thank you so much for being here.

Jordan Firstman: Thank you for having me.

I’ve been getting a lot of press alerts about your outfits, so I feel like you’ve been really on a tour.

I’m really glad to hear that because I’ve had some looks I’m proud of.

What was the first fashion show you ever went to?

During the pandemic, I was the virtual host of a Thom Browne fashion show.

I played a newscaster, and that was my first fashion-related thing. I think the first show I went to was randomly Vetements. They sat me next to Edward Enninful and someone else fancy, and I was living. But it was exciting to be at a fashion show.

It is exciting because it’s like theater for people with ADD. You sit, you wait, you’re excited, and then 12 minutes later, it’s done.

And you’re like, “Oh, I witnessed this cultural experience, and I didn’t have to sit through two and a half hours and an intermission.”

It’s true. I didn’t have to watch a whole feature film. You’re so mad at me for making a movie. You’re like, “Why wasn’t it a short?”

I find it to be. I’m proud that, in the beginning screenings, I wasn’t telling people the runtime. I’d ask them afterward, and they’d say, “It felt like 1:40.”

I went with my 23-year-old club-kid colleague, and it was as if I were watching a foreign film. Edward was translating for me. We also discovered afterward that Edward had received an email asking him to be an extra.

Every gay in New York City did. It’s very much that Madison Beer meme: “I was supposed to be in the video.” Every gay guy in New York.

We had two amazing producers I brought on, Zach Stone and Ben Hubley, who were already in the party scene. I couldn’t have done it without them.

I went to college with Zach Stone, but anyway…

He’s great. He’s the best. They basically sent out mass texts and emails to everyone they’d ever partied with, and people showed up. It was actually a beautiful part of the process, seeing the community show up for creativity. It moved me to see everyone in one space together. They were there to have a good time and party.

I want to know what your relationship with club culture is. I think of you as an LA person, both because of I Love LA and before. Why did you set this in New York club culture rather than LA club culture?

To me, New York club culture has so much history. We’re standing on the backs of giants. From Studio 54 to the ’80s to the actual Club Kids days in the ’90s, it has such a lineage and such a vibe. LA has things going on, but it’s a bit less specific. I also think the idea of marathon partying has changed. I say in the movie, “It’s the Berlinification of New York, mama.” I think that’s happened, where marathon-style partying, starting on Friday and going until Sunday, is a new thing for New York.

Yeah. People really stay out all night. You end up at an afters, then go to another party. I don’t think it’s really meant to be in New York because New York isn’t Berlin. You have to hustle all week. You have to work really hard. I just heard a girl in the Vogue bathroom screaming at someone, “You need to keep your phone on!” So there’s a different vibe. She’s going to watch this and be like, “Oh, shit.”

But I think there’s a different grind in this city. When you put that next to the party scene, it creates a hamster wheel that I think a lot of gay men are living through, loving, but also having problems with. It was interesting for me to set the movie here. Also, New York and a kid are cinematic. There’s a lineage of movies like this that feel cozy, movies I wanted to replicate from the ’70s, like Kramer vs. Kramer.

Gloria, Kramer vs. Kramer, and obviously Big Daddy, which we’ve gotten a lot of comparisons to. There’s also a movie called One Fine Day. Do you remember that?

That was a visual reference. Uptown Girls, obviously. Such a classic. I wanted to be part of that canon, and I felt like a queer retelling of the story was deserved and made sense. We have this delayed coming of age as gay men. We don’t have the same pressures to have kids or settle down, so we keep partying. But eventually that becomes an issue, even for your body. It’s a hard burden to carry, continuing to party every weekend.

When I’ve taken writing classes, they always say that novelists write what they know in their first novel. They write something that feels true. What’s the germ of inspiration for this story? I don’t think you actually have a club kid, but where are you coming from?

It came from a very simple idea. I was at a dinner party with friends who had an eight-year-old son. I was saying inappropriate things in front of him and making him laugh, and the parents were laughing too. I thought there might be something funny in the dynamic between me and a kid.

I feel like a kid in a lot of ways. I think I have a childlike spirit, and I’ve always gotten along with kids. I really like them and relate to them. That was the germ of the idea. Then I had a boyfriend in Berlin, so I was there a lot, partying. It was really fun, but the comedowns were hard, and I think it took away from things.

2021–2024. I basically wrote the first draft before the breakup, and it got really good after the breakup. I’ve been calling it my Adele breakup album.

It is a breakup movie in a lot of ways. There’s a feeling of love in the movie, and I think that comes from the love I had and have for my ex, the times we spent together, and the parties we had together. I see it as a love letter to him. We haven’t spoken since, and I hear he’s doing well. I want him to do well. I felt like I had a lot of love to put on the page, and that’s when it got really good.

I read that you crashed real parties during filming and brought crew members with you. What did that look like? Paint the scene.

I didn’t crash. There were weeks of discussion with the party planners. My friend Noah Shakoor throws a party called Pit Stop, and he was like, “Come shoot the party.” Really, all you have to do is put up a sign saying you’re being filmed. There’s also a very famous afters in New York that goes until 3:00 p.m. the next day. It starts at 7:00 p.m. on Saturday and ends at 3:00 p.m. Sunday.

What do you do for fake bundle or kundle?

There’s actually a funny story here. There’s a scene where I’m supposed to be selling drugs at the party.

For listeners at home, bundle is cocaine.

Bundle is the original. Everything stems from bundle. Kundle is K, gundle is GHB, which I heard you didn’t know about.

You shouldn’t try GHB. I love you, but I don’t think you should try that drug.

I’ve been told I’d be even more insane. People have said I have no chill.

I think molly is good for you. I think you’re a molly girl.

Feel it out. Feel the music. Hug someone. That’s the vibe. Mundle, molly.

Now there are all the numbers—3-MMC, 4-MMC—so thrundle, frundle.

This is too much. You’re supposed to remember this when you’re high?

Everything is undle, so you just add the first initial.

What about ayahuasca? Is there ayawundle?

Oh, wow. I’m going to be using that all week.

I’m imagining the Woody Allen big sneeze scene. Tell me about people doing fake cocaine.

Here’s the story. I was selling fake drugs, and people knew there was a camera there, but they didn’t really know what was happening. They thought something else. They were high. I gave one girl a bump, and she said, “What the fuck? That’s not K.” She started getting really mad at me. I told her it was fake drugs, just powdered lactose. She said, “I’m lactose intolerant.” I actually ended up drugging someone with fake drugs by giving them that.

I had powdered vitamin D or C and powdered lactose. I found that the lactose looked the most like coke. The vitamin C looked more like K. It was a little saltier-looking. There’s a lot of trickery. Diego, our props guy, shout-out. What a fun job for the props department.

We talk a lot at Vogue about the different etiquette for different situations. What is club etiquette?

I think club etiquette is actually very boundaried and respectful. If you lose control at the club, it’s not a good look. Especially in Berlin. When I was new to Berlin, my friend was DJing behind the decks. I was trying to say hi and get his attention, and someone told me no. It’s a no-no to distract the DJ. There are definitely rules. You don’t want to be messy. Having a good attitude is important, too. You don’t want to be a bitch.

Anytime I’m in a group and people have an attitude, I’m like, “What are we doing here?” We’re here to have a good time. Be open to new people. Read the room. If someone doesn’t want to talk to you, move on. Those are my rules at the club.

Those are good rules. You also cast a lot of people who are club habitués. How did you find these individuals? What was it like working with people who aren’t actors? This was also your first directing experience.

I did everything they say you shouldn’t do on your first film. I worked with a kid, worked with non-actors, shot on film, shot at real parties, and shot in New York. There were days when I thought, Why did I do this to myself? But as far as the non-actors go, they just came. We had so much history together by that point. We were friends, and I’d been partying with Saturn for years. I’d also partied with Alaska [Riley].

She always felt like such a maternal figure in the LA party scene, but also had this power and confidence while being warm. I always wanted that for the character. The movie is about the different types of families we can create. Saffron is a mother figure to Arlo in a lot of ways.

She shockingly convinced me, as someone with a four- and six-year-old, that it was a good idea for him to DJ.

That’s the trick of the movie. You see it and you’re like, “Sure, we’re making this argument.” Then the second time, you’re like, “This is a terrible plan.” That was intentional. I wanted you to feel like you’re watching this kid learn and express himself creatively, and you’re like, “Yes, yes, yes.” Then you’re like, “No, no, no.”

It’s interesting to think about because there’s obviously a way to nurture creativity, even in a DJ setting, without actually bringing a kid to the club. There are so many merits to having these queer ideas in a kid’s life, while also being realistic and practical. That’s the whole thing with Peter. He’s doing the baseline of parenting, which is love. He’s also a pushover to everyone, especially Arlo. He just wants Arlo to have everything he wants.

I love him. This kid is such a star. I hear he also teased and bullied you.

I gave him permission. He would say things like, “You’re being really cringe right now,” or, “That’s such a dad joke.” I became the embarrassing dad to him. Now I do things to make him cringe because I enjoy it. I feel like a dad to him sometimes, and it’s fun. I think that’s what made him comfortable on set: being able to make fun of me.

It’s hard to work with a young person in that way, and also to get to know them.

That’s one thing I hope people take away from the movie: having a more honest relationship with kids. It’s something I wish I’d had when I was younger. I didn’t know my parents were people. That never occurred to me. I don’t think they really saw me as a person, either. They saw me as their kid. I wish I’d known more about their struggles or what they were feeling inside. I think it would’ve taught me more about what life was going to be like. We have these barriers between parents and kids that I think we could soften a little.

I want to know whether Reggie is actually into music. I was impressed with how seamless it was.

Yes, majorly. But his music taste has completely changed. He’s at that age where he’s impressionable. He came in loving Slipknot and Metallica. He was like, “I like the hard stuff.” Now he loves Cocteau Twins and Massive Attack. His whole playlist has changed. We have a shared playlist now.

Wow. Did you start that during the movie?

We started it a bit after the movie, but obviously the movie inspired it. It’s really sweet to watch him change through this experience. Watching him start doing press and interviews, he’s become so mature, grown-up, and funny. I feel like a proud parent. I understand why parents cry watching the school play. You’re like, “Oh my God, this is my kid. He’s up there doing it, and he’s so good.”

He’s so good. I hear you guys have been DJing together.

He DJs, I’m the hype man. I’m in the back. I don’t know all the knobs and stuff. Saturn taught him the basics. He knows his highs, lows, and mids.

Jordan Firstman, Reggie Absolom, and Saturn Risin9 at the after-party for the Los Angeles premiere of Club Kid.

Absolutely. I also heard that you brought the straight film crew to Basement and were teaching them some lingo. What was that Duolingo lesson like?

Duolingo, cundle edition. We need to get the Duolingo owl.

That’s an A24 idea. Are you here? That’s a really good idea. Pay her some money. You have a good job; you don’t need the extra funds. I’ll take the Duolingo license.

The question was about bringing your straight crew to Basement and teaching everyone.

They just had the best time. It’s not like they’d never partied before, but exposing them to the exact type of queer people the movie was about was important. I wanted everyone to deeply understand the details. The movie comes alive with the details, even the types of furniture a New York gay guy has in his apartment. We have Butt magazine, and we have our own specific things.

A lot of chrome right now. There’s one kind of chain-link table that a lot of gay guys have. It’s a lot of chrome and black. Black leather couch. Chic, but also a little grimy.

I want to know if you ever considered having someone else play Peter.

Keanu Reeves. No, this was always my goal and my dream. I thought of people like Lena Dunham, Donald Glover, Phoebe Waller-Bridge. I knew I had a voice, and I knew I could act a bit, so it was always the plan.

I’m always impressed with people who can do all three. You wrote it, directed it, and acted in it. How did you move between those three roles?

I tried to think of it like Pandora’s box. The movie was the box, and everything went into it. All my jobs were funneling into the project. I tried not to separate my actor brain from my writer brain or my director brain. If I did that, I’d start to freak out and lose control of the whole thing. Everything was in service of getting all the ideas, vision, and craft into one thing.

That’s such a good question. I think it’s both a mistake I made and something I don’t regret. You can tell in a club scene when people are faking dancing. I had a looped beat and thought we should dance to it to get the energy up. My sound guy said we really needed to do takes without sound because the edit would be a nightmare. The edit was a nightmare because you have to go beat by beat. But the crowd had more energy because the music was playing. It was a double-edged sword: harder in the edit, but better for the movie.

You’ve cast a lot of your friends in your projects. Do you ever find it difficult to work with friends? Is it harder to give direction?

I found that both the party host in me and the people-pleaser in me conflicted with directing. I wanted everyone to have a good time. Part of shooting is doing a lot of takes. It’s not comfortable and it’s annoying. Some of my friends didn’t realize that they’d do a scene full-out, and I’d say, “That’s the wide, and we’re not really going to use the wide.” By the time we got to their coverage, they didn’t have the same energy as they did in the wide.

Especially in those group scenes, where I had every cool gay guy in New York, excluding your friend who didn’t show up to work. I felt bad asking them to do 10 takes of dancing. They were sweaty and tired and they weren’t getting paid that much. That was the hardest part: getting what I needed as a director while keeping everyone happy.

I want to know about your crazy T-shirt collection. That was one of my favorite things. We’ve been talking a lot on the Vogue fashion team about how there’s a real slogan T-shirt renaissance right now.

What’s your favorite slogan T-shirt in the rotation right now?

I have some things I’m making. We made an “Innit Babes” one for the movie. We’re going to make a “Mama, Let’s Research” one.

I saw you made “I Boofed at Cannes and All I Got Was This Lousy Shirt.”

That was a good one. I’m going to go with “I Boofed at Cannes” because people didn’t understand what either of the two T-shirts I made for Cannes meant. There was “I Need a Doll Line and a Sickening Dose Stat” and “I Boofed at Cannes and All I Got Was This Lousy Shirt.” The beauty of them was that no one understood either of them.

I loved your character in I Love LA. You’re a stylist. What did you do to research for that role? Are there stylists you look to?

There’s one stylist whose aesthetic I’d been looking at. I won’t say who it is. In LA, you’re around a lot of creative people. Being friends with Charli, you see her whole glam team. Makeup people and hair people have their own personalities. Stylists have their own personalities.

I’ve been around a lot of stylists, so I was channeling some specific behaviors. But I was also thinking about the loneliness you can have as a gay stylist. You’re basically a paid best friend to these celebrities. You’re there when they need you, but then at a certain point you have to leave and go do more work for them. Sometimes they yell at you. Sometimes you mess up, and sometimes things aren’t perfect. It’s a hard job being a stylist, and you don’t get a lot of gratitude from the world or sometimes even the people you work with.

I Love LA has started production on season two, or not yet?

Ended. It comes out very soon. I don’t think I can say the date, but soon. Sooner than you could ever imagine.

What’s the vibe on set with that crew? Do you have group chats? How much are you guys in touch?

All the time. We’ve become family, and the set is so easy and fun. We improvise, help each other with our looks, and it’s definitely family vibes now.

I want to know what your cultural diet is right now. Have you seen the Elizabeth Holmes documentary?

I have. I was in the room at Telluride when they dropped it.

It was a pure, unadulterated gag. I can’t remember the last time I was squeezing someone’s hand like that. I couldn’t believe it. The “Who’s on First?” thing really got me.

Sorry. Never mind. It was a once-in-a-lifetime kind of thing. It only would have worked with those two people together. There aren’t two other people who could make that movie work. I think it’s a real accomplishment.

Remi Wolf. Her new album is so good. She has a song called “I Won’t Cry” that’s one of the best love songs I’ve ever heard. I’m also getting into the new Troye Sivan album. “Fucking Forever,” another good love song. I’m newly in love, maybe, so I’m into love songs right now.

What’s the dream date when you’re newly in love?

I actually like a party. I love a classic walk. If we’re in Paris, walking, eating, and sitting by the river is always romantic. New York, too. A little rain never hurt anyone. I love a first date with kissing. Sitting at a bar for a long time and just kissing is really hot to me.

For a gay guy, it’s kind of transgressive to only kiss on a first date. It’s sexy not to know what’s going on underneath the pants and just keep it to mouth stuff. I also like going to the club with someone I love, doing a little molly, and making out. That’s really sweet and fun to me.

Okay. Let’s do it. Then I have to run upstairs.

Who is the worst type of person to party with?

Who’s the best type of person to party with?

Strappy. We’ve seen it. Strappy and midriff. We’ve seen it.

I’m such a gay guy. I think a white tank top is hot and looks good. A black tank top, too. Shorts. Athletic shorts are so hot at the club.

3:00 to 4:00 a.m. I think it’s a really cool hour. Things get a little loosey-goosey, but not cracky.

That’s when you want loosey-goosey, not cracky.

Loosey-goosey, not cracky-wacky. You’re not only learning lingo, you’re inventing it. I’m helping gay culture. You’re really pushing the culture forward.

An espresso martini at the club is kind of a vibe.

That doesn’t conflict with the mundle or the trundle?

If you’re doing G, you can’t drink anything. If I’m being real, a crisp Diet Coke. Or a mate. In Berlin, they have Club-Mate. Mate and vodka is really nice.

Favorite post-club snack? This is where our interests can overlap.

You know what? I like a soup. Something nourishing, like a vegetable soup or pho. You want to go fried, but your body actually wants something nourishing.

Let’s go pho. You say to someone, “Let’s go pho. Let’s get out of here and go pho.”

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6640. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6639. All About Luciana Damon, Matt Damon’s Wife of More Than 20 Years

Matt Damon may be one of Hollywood’s biggest stars, but his love story started far from a movie set.

The actor met his wife, Luciana Damon (née Barroso), in 2003 while filming Stuck on You in Miami. At the time, she was a bartender, and what began as an unexpected meeting eventually grew into a long-lasting marriage.

More than two decades later, the couple shares four daughters, has worked together professionally behind the scenes, and continues to make family a priority—even as Matt’s career takes him around the world. Most recently, Luciana and their daughters joined him at the London and New York premieres of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.

Here’s everything to know about Luciana Damon.

Luciana was born in Argentina and later moved to the United States.

While she has largely stayed out of the public eye throughout her marriage, she gave a rare interview to Vogue Australia in 2018, offering a glimpse into her family life and relationship with Matt.

Matt and Luciana first crossed paths in 2003 while he was filming Stuck on You in Miami.

Matt has often described it as love at first sight. During a 2011 appearance on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, he recalled, “I literally saw her across a crowded room, literally. Eight years and four kids later, that’s my life. I don’t know how else our paths would’ve crossed if that didn’t happen.”

Luciana remembers the evening a little differently.

“Matt’s story is that he saw me across the room, and there was a light on me. And I’m like, ‘Yeah, it was a nightclub—there were lights everywhere!’” she told Vogue Australia.

She explained that Matt came behind the bar after fans began approaching him for photos and autographs.

“He had started getting recognized and asked for pictures and autographs, and then it got kind of aggressive because people are drinking and stuff,” she said. “So he came and hid behind the bar...[wanting to] just hang out back there and have a drink. He says, ‘Oh, I saw you, and I really wanted to talk to you.’”

Rather than letting him stand around, she gave him a job.

“I said: ‘You know, if you’re going to be back here, you can’t just be standing there!’” she recalled. “He had trained as a bartender for a film years before, so he started making drinks. And he made me a ton of money in tips that night, because of course everyone wanted to go and see him. So it turned into a really fun night and then 15 years later, here we are!”

Luciana was raising her daughter, Alexia, from a previous relationship when she met Matt.

She told Vogue Australia that when Matt invited her to continue the evening with him and his friends, she declined because she needed to get home.

“I was like, ‘I can’t, I have a four-year-old daughter, I’m not going anywhere’...and that was one of the things he loved, that I had a daughter,” she said.

“He said, ‘I love that you’re a mom and that’s your priority.’ Some guys might have been different, they might think it’s complicated, but for him it wasn’t. When you meet somebody that you have a connection with, that’s just the person that you have a connection with, all the other stuff—the movie-star part—wasn’t really a factor. It was just Matt, to me he’s just Matt.”

The couple later welcomed three daughters together—Isabella, Gia, and Stella—and Matt has long considered Alexia his own daughter as well.

After dating for roughly two years, Matt and Luciana married in a private ceremony in December 2005.

Their wedding bands carry a particularly meaningful family tradition. Speaking to Parade in 2017, Matt explained that the rings contain tiny diamonds from his grandparents’ wedding ring.

“They weren’t quality diamonds; it was what [my grandfather] could afford,” he said. “But the marriage lasted. They were married for over 60 years. It wasn’t about the ring; it was about the marriage.”

“So when I told my mother that I was marrying Lucy, she gave me that ring and there were these six little diamonds. We took three of them and we put them on the inside of my band, and then we took three and we put them on the inside of her band. So they’re not visible, but we’re hopefully carrying the best part of that union with us.”

Over the years, Matt has shared one relationship rule that has helped their marriage endure.

“We have a two-week rule,” he told YourTango in 2021. “I’m not away for more than two weeks. I think you need to be with the person you love as much as possible. My wife is my soulmate. I don’t like being apart from her.”

There have been rare exceptions. While promoting Oppenheimer in 2023, Matt joked to Entertainment Weekly that he negotiated a break from acting with one exception.

“I had—not to get too personal—negotiated extensively with my wife that I was taking time off,” he said. “The one caveat to my taking time off was if Chris Nolan called.”

Matt has repeatedly credited Luciana with helping him navigate both his career and life.

During an interview with Jake’s Takes in 2023, he recalled feeling discouraged while filming a movie that wasn’t turning out the way he’d hoped.

“I remember my wife pulling me up because I fell into a depression,” he said.

Matt added, “I do pride myself, in a large part because of her, at being a professional actor. And what being a professional actor means is you go and you do the 15-hour day and give it absolutely everything, even in what you know is going to be a losing effort. If you can do that with the best possible attitude, then you’re a pro. And she really helped me with that.”

Although Luciana wasn’t part of the entertainment industry when she met Matt, she’s taken on a larger role behind the camera in recent years.

She served as an executive producer on The Instigators in 2024 and produced The Rip in 2026.

Speaking with Entertainment Tonight at The Instigators premiere, Matt said the producing credit had been years in the making.

“She’s been reading every script and watching every cut of every movie for 21 years. This is the first time we ever kind of codified it,” he said.

He added that Luciana initially resisted taking credit for her work.

“She didn’t even want to take the credit. She was there every day, she was doing all this work on the script, and then she was like, ‘Nah, I don’t want to take the credit.’”

“The other producers on the movie...came of their own volition [and said], ‘If you’re not taking credit, we’re not taking credit.’ It was very sweet. She succumbed and took the credit.”

Luciana has rarely spoken publicly about her marriage, but when Vogue Australia asked about the secret to a lasting relationship, her answer was refreshingly simple.

“I just know I think we both feel, really, really lucky to have met each other so we don’t take that for granted. It’s life and marriage, so there’s ups and downs you know, but overall it’s easy and it’s fun. And he’s such a good dad.”

In a November 2026 interview with GQ, Matt revealed that Luciana underwent brain surgery after experiencing a brain aneurysm in 2024.

“She’s totally fine, thank God, but [she] had this brain surgery the week before the Oscars,” he said.

Although the couple missed the ceremony, Luciana surprised Matt by getting dressed up to attend an Oscars after-party once she was feeling better.

“But it was the first night she felt good enough to get up and had her energy back. And she surprised me and got a dress and we went out to the after-party, because she remembered that the last time it happened, I didn’t do it. And she was like, ‘This time we’re going out.’ And it was pretty fucking heroic of her to do that and really meaningful,” Damon recalled.
