#6638. Inside the NYC Members' Club Where Republicans and Democrats Party Together

A half-dozen of us are squeezed into a small service elevator, our various colognes clashing with the signature fish-and-rubber scent of Lower Manhattan. The elevator operator blares Chinese ballads, and the young man next to me bobs his head in appreciation. An older man shifts uncomfortably. “Could you actually make it louder?” he snarks. Over the course of one excruciatingly slow ride to the sixth floor, we’re trapped in our private discomfort or pleasure. But we’re all headed to the same place: a midterms watch party at The Bench, a members’ club for people who are into politics but feel like political outsiders. It’s a place, according to its website, where “restless organizers, creatives, misfits, sneakerheads, and policy nerds collide.”

Since its founding two years ago, The Bench has hosted insiders ranging from CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Monthly dues, “just to keep the lights on,” run as little as $50. The space is regularly used for events unaffiliated with The Bench: readings by literary magazines, climate week pop-ups, splashy debates. Michka Bengio, the social club’s owner and co-founder, is an earnest believer in dialogue and, if his programming is any indication, a little bit of a chaos agent. He likes to produce scenarios that underscore political tensions, like when he had Weiss’s The Free Press, co-host a watch party for Mamdani’s 2025 election. According to those who attended, it was a somber evening for the pro-Cuomo crowd, though some of them nevertheless returned to The Bench for this week’s midterms viewing.

On the night of the midterm elections, partygoers had the option of viewing the election results in a spacious, orderly room displaying CNN’s broadcast or in a lounge-y, narrower space screening Fox News’s coverage. In a cozy hallway between the two screens, guests could buy cocktails and popcorn or engage with people whose political views differ from their own—arguably The Bench’s most exclusive offering.

“There’s just a whole splatter of different opinions that come in here,” says David Azoulay, who works with the content agency Fixer Media. “The Free Press, the Manhattan Institute, and then I also get to meet a lot of people who are working in the Democratic space, on the Biden or Kamala Harris campaigns.” Azoulay helped produce events for an “America 250” tour in collaboration with Young America’s Foundation, a conservative youth organization, and has worked with provocateur Ben Shapiro and former Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Though he used to be a registered Democrat, he “grew up” and now identifies as a proud Republican. While Azoulay engaged in a playful back-and-forth with a progressive 21-year-old over what he considers to be the fallacy of socialism, Democratic councilmember Christopher Marte milled about wearing an “I Voted” sticker.

Over the sound of people screaming about the James Talarico-Ken Paxton race, Marte told me he met Bengio 10 years ago through Arena, a New York-based political organization that took off in the wake of the first Trump presidency. “It was all these young people trying to figure out how to get involved in politics. A.O.C. was on the couch, Alessandra Biaggi, all these people who were just curious, post-Trump election,” he says. At the time, Bengio was working as a campaign manager for Michael Basch, a techno-optimistic Democratic NYC mayoral candidate, a gig he secured by asking the only person he knew in politics to introduce them. He’s also worked as a consultant for NBA Africa and managed downtown restaurants like Regina’s Grocery and Miss Lily’s. The Bench is one of four Bengio ventures; he also co-founded the supper club Shtick with his wife, Jacqueline Lobel, and partners with the Hancock Foundation and the Hancock Cafe. On any given event night, he can be found buzzing around the room, excitedly facilitating introductions for his guests.

The son of a Moroccan father and Algerian mother, Bengio grew up in Strasbourg, France. When I ask what motivated him to move to New York in 2001, he deadpans: “Ever heard of the American dream?” More specifically, though, he was jealous of a friend who moved to the States for six months and returned speaking fluent English. “He was the coolest kid,” Bengio says. “And I was like, ‘I want to go to America, too.’ I love basketball,” he says, reorganizing a pile of books so that the edges aligned just so.

Bengio, a first-time voter, is coy about his own politics. Instead, he’s driven by the promise of America “that you can coexist,” he says, and a desire to nurture civil, democratic debate. “I want to be part of the project.”

“We need to really recommit and reaffirm what we mean when we talk about free speech—expression that is unencumbered by political interference in any way, shape, or form,” says Josef Palermo, a former curator at the Kennedy Center who drove up from the nation’s capital to attend this party. Earlier this year, Palermo wrote about the politicization of the Kennedy Center by both the Biden and Trump administrations in an article for The Atlantic. “We need spaces like this in D.C. Everybody’s in their own camps and certain venues are definitely coded one way or the other. I think having something like this would be huge in our nation’s capital.”

Then again, it’s partly New York’s distance from the D.C. swamp that makes talking about politics at The Bench feel cool. The space is decorated with Bengio’s enviable collection of NBA and political memorabilia. (He jokes that he stays up late scrolling vintage sites and bidding on Americana rarities.) Alongside Michael Jordan Wheaties boxes and a slew of rare basketball sneakers, there’s a framed copy of Emile Zola’s 1897 letter to the French youth during the Dreyfus affair, a portable Florida voting booth from the Bush vs. Gore election, a framed paper shift dress from Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign, and nearly every issue of John F. Kennedy Jr’s George magazine. The one with a Donald Trump cover gets taken down from the wall often, Bengio says, but he always puts it back up.

On Tuesday night, there appeared to be other collectors of rare political merch. Vintage Obama-era crop tops caught my eye, and a speechwriter for a New York City council member waxed poetic about his favorite vinyl record: a collection of John F. Kennedy speeches. Two guys wore t-shirts they designed themselves that cheekily quoted Michigan turncoat Haley Stevens: “Israel cums to me in my dreams.” (One of them requested anonymity, fearful of being cancelled by the Canary Mission, an anonymous organization that tracks critics of Israel.)

A good number of attendees who were professionally invested in the election outcomes couldn’t stop checking their phones. Anthony DiMieri, the man behind Mamdani’s winning social media strategy, told me he’d just come from Brad Lander’s party. Max Altman, the brother of the OpenAI founder Sam, also stopped by. He’s excited about a recent move to New York from Austin, Texas, and if he hadn’t forgotten to request an absentee ballot, he says, he would’ve voted for James Talarico.

As the results turned progressively blue, the room began to clear out. Before leaving, I chatted with Azoulay’s “libertarian friend” Hunt Beaty. In the hallway between broadcasts, Beaty tells me he’s not terribly moved by the midterms. “Everything interesting that is happening in the world right now, to me, is happening outside of politics,” he says. He rejects the libertarian designation and lives by the credo “free minds and free markets,” citing Reason magazine. And yet, Beaty finds that The Bench still has something to offer him.

“It’s fun to be in a room filled with buzzy, interesting people who at least are able to try and talk about ideas, while also being like, ‘Maybe we’re doing coke in the bathroom, too.’ I want there to be a New York City where those things could coexist.”

#6637. I Flew United Polaris To Try Its Chef's Table Menu—And Didn't Expect To Enjoy Dinner This Much

From chilled crab soup to coffee-glazed short ribs, this was hardly your typical airplane meal.

With airlines constantly trying to one-up each other in premium cabins, United is hoping its food can give it an edge. As part of a broader overhaul of its food and beverage program, the airline introduced chef-created meals for United Polaris, its international business class, through a collaboration with Chef's Table.

I wrote about the menus when they were first announced, so naturally I was curious when I had the chance to actually eat one myself on an overnight flight from Newark to Edinburgh.

I’ve flown up front on a handful of other airlines, but this was my first time in Polaris—and I planned to approach it like any other overnight flight: Eat dinner, get comfortable, and pass out until Europe.

Before the flight, I preordered the Chef’s Table menu created by Fariyal Abdullahi, chef partner at New York City’s Hav & Mar. And while I don’t find myself eating at ultra-luxury restaurants all that often—I did eventually make it to a Michelin-starred one once I landed in Edinburgh—having a meal like this at 35,000 feet felt like a treat.

Abdullahi says her menu was guided by “two pillars that inform all my cooking: geography and seasonality.” Tomatoes and endive nodded to what was in season around New York and New Jersey, while other parts of the meal pulled directly from her Ethiopian roots. The pepitas were seasoned with berbere, and the short ribs were braised with coffee, nodding to Ethiopia’s connection to the ingredient.

Of course, creating a restaurant dish and serving one several miles above the ground are two very different assignments. Aaron McMillan, United’s Managing Director of Hospitality Programs, told me the airline considers everything from ingredients and preparation to presentation when adapting a chef’s recipe for the air. The goal, he says, is to preserve what makes the original dish work while ensuring it can be prepared and served consistently onboard.

Because this was an overnight flight, my appetizer, salad, and entree arrived together, which was honestly ideal. I wanted to eat, settle in, and begin the nightly debate over whether I was actually going to sleep.

Cold soup on a plane? Crab on a plane? Those are two concepts I would ordinarily approach with at least a little caution, but this ended up being one of the highlights of the meal.

The tomato soup had plenty of actual tomato flavor without being watery or oily, and there was enough crab that it didn’t feel like somebody had sprinkled three sad pieces on top and called it a day. It tasted like real crab, too, rather than the imitation stuff that would have immediately made the whole thing feel considerably less special.

More importantly, the two actually worked together. I went into this course most prepared to question my life choices and instead finished basically all of it.

I love a big meal as much as the next person, but eating something rich immediately before trying to sleep on a plane can be a dangerous game. So I was grateful to see some greenery sharing the tray.

The salad combined baby gem and endive with berbere-spiced pepitas, dried cranberries, pecorino Romano, and a creamy anchovy vinaigrette.

The cranberries brought some sweetness against the salty pecorino and vinaigrette, while the pepitas gave everything the crunch a pile of airplane greens desperately needs. And if “anchovy vinaigrette” has you picturing a salad that tastes aggressively fishy, this wasn’t that. The dressing had enough punch to make it interesting without overpowering everything underneath it.

If it isn’t already obvious, this was not the most photogenic meal I’ve ever been served. Purple mashed potatoes topped with glazed short ribs under airplane lighting don't necessarily set anyone up for Instagram greatness—but don’t judge a Chef’s Table entree by its cover.

The short ribs were extremely tender and came apart easily, which is especially appreciated when your dining room is an airplane seat and you don’t particularly want to start sawing away at a piece of meat with tiny cutlery. They also weren’t overly fatty, something that can quickly ruin short ribs for me.

Alongside the purple mashed potatoes were sautéed Thumbelina carrots and charred scallions, and everything worked together without any one element taking over the plate.

Saucy short ribs and mashed potatoes right before several more hours trapped on an airplane can also make you start mentally mapping the location of every bathroom pretty quickly, but thankfully, I wasn’t punished for my confidence.

United set out to make its airplane food something passengers might actually remember after landing, and at least on this flight, the Chef’s Table program feels like a pretty convincing step in that direction.

The cabin around me may have been showing its age a little, but dinner certainly wasn’t.

#6636. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6633. All the Wardrobe Essentials Every Guy Should Own in 2026

When it comes to getting dressed, we often rhapsodize about the virtues of “wardrobe essentials for men” as if everyone knows what we mean. So, let's actually talk about it.

On Maslow's hierarchy of menswear needs, wardrobe essentials might begin the perfect white tee, a killer pair of jeans, and the shoes you can wear with them. But in compiling this list, our goal wasn’t simply to meet your needs—you are, frankly, a grown-ass man, and hopefully have those covered—but more to remind you of the fundamental pieces of menswear that have helped men look hotter and feel better for generations. And in a world of non-stop trends, we need these reminders now more than ever.

In aggregate, our essentials constitute the foundation of a rock-solid men’s basic wardrobe. Below, a highly specific starter pack of everything you’ll want—nay, need—to wear in the year of our lord 2026.

A plain white T-shirt can be worn as an undershirt, standalone with some vintage jeans, or—if you want to get DIY—screen-printed into a work of art. Looking for an indie version no one else has? Check out our guide to the best white tees.

Slim, abbreviated trunks or boxer briefs that keep everything in place are the foundation of every rock-solid wardrobe—whether other people can see ‘em or not. Even if you’re in the minority that’s committed to boxer shorts, it pays to spend a little more on something that’s, you know, holding your balls all day long.

We love the zany knitwear options flooding the internet these days. But if we're honest, there will always be a spot in our closets for a classic crewneck sweater. They're timeless and endlessly style-able, even if you only manage to drape one across your shoulders.

There's a reason that the Levi's 501s is at the very top of our guide to the best men's jeans: it has been, is, and always will be the jeans you come back to again (and again, and again). If you dig your denim light and a little looser, though, Gap's Loose Jeans are a close second. Can't think of what to wear? Here's your answer, seven days a week.

If there’s another theme here, it’s that menswear essentials shouldn’t be unitaskers. They should be useful in a variety of situations, and when it comes to tailoring in particular, the navy blazer is a Swiss Army Knife. It works in almost any situation, from job interviews (with a tie) to weddings (someone else's or your own). Bonus points if you opt for a double-breasted number with strong shoulders, brash peak lapels, and an unmistakable sense of what Italians—and menswear guys—call sprezzatura.

The menswear-sphere admittedly overloaded on loafers, and we’re now seeing a slight shift in the shoe zeitgeist. But that doesn’t take away from the fact that the right pair of loafers can still be the most versatile kicks in your closet. They’ve got more range than Daniel Day-Lewis and can go from casual to dressy to punk in a flash. Wear 'em with socks or without, and count yourself lucky when they get truly worn in—then keep wearing them.

Sure, everyone knows a guy who refuses to wear shorts. But he's overpowered every time by his greatest foes: Those months of the year where, honestly, wearing anything but a short becomes a compromise. Our favorite pairs merge style with practicality, and only look better the more thrashed they get. (Except for the Champion shorts—maybe keep those a little cleaner.)

They may have emerged from the sweaty, stylish world of sportswear, but hoodies have long since transcended their athletic origins. These ones have the stamina to take you from a coffee run to casual Friday at the office (just put it under one of those jean jackets we're always telling you about).

We get that simple sneakers aren’t exactly the type of kicks you lust after on StockX, but there’s no denying the rush of dopamine you get when you break out a fresh pair, or how well they go with literally everything. At less than a Benjamin there's the Converse Chuck Taylor, a mainstay of our sneakers coverage, since, uh, always.

Not ready to take the plunge on a serious diver from Rolex or Omega? You're in luck: Seiko's much-heralded 5 series gives you everything you could want in a dive watch—an automatic movement, a day-date display, water resistance, and a near-indestructible case—at a price that won't require a second mortgage. (If you've got a few more dollars to play around with, Hamilton is no slouch, either.)

Like a plain white tee or simple white crew socks, a white Oxford shirt is a true workhorse. It can take the 9-to-5 like a champ, sharpen up for a fancier occasion, or kick back wide open over your favorite vintage tee. If you only have one shirt with buttons, let it be this.

Remember chinos? The wardrobe staple of preppies and, inexplicably, grandpas everywhere? The pant that taps in when your jeans need a break? The ones that Gap viral-ized in the late-90s? These days chinos are back and bigger than before. The chinos of today are surprisingly familiar and look more like the military-issued pairs of the midcentury—high rise and hella roomy. Some even have a pleat or two. We're all for going wide and pleated, but these both present a happy-ish medium.

While people usually start talking about them in April, sunglasses are a year-round necessity—overcast January skies be damned. They’re relevant whether you’re soaking up the summer rays, trying to cut the wintry glare, or simply trying to navigate life with a little more stealth.

Headwear trends come and go—we see you, crochet knit beanies and Trucker hats—but the baseball cap is eternal. You wear one, your dad wears one, your grandpa wears one. The solution for everything from a bad hair day, to an impromptu work Zoom, to forgetting to pack your sunglasses, they're also just plain cool, whether brand new or a little worn out. Always have been, always will.

Sweatpants should be cozy, sure, but the best of the genre are so much more than mere lazy-Sunday garb. We’ve moved past the calf-gripping elastane-pumped versions that have defined the closets of so many Lulu bros and dudes who have skate decks hung up as art. Instead, sweatpants now should be closer to the originals with a baggier fit and even wide-open hems. Spring for a pair that oozes Rocky-level charm, and they'll become the bed-to-bodega bottoms you can't stop wearing outside of the house, too.

There were a few years where the collective menswear consciousness leaned into “fun socks,” and further away from God. How easily we are led astray… Thankfully, we all now agree that the best socks are really the ones you forget that you're wearing, because they're so quietly consistent and comfortable. And in all of our years of reporting on savvy men's style choices, we've never heard a bad word said against any of the four contenders below.

Sometimes clothes can make you feel like you’re living a movie, and a good trench coat is like you’re aiming for an Oscar. (Those trucker jackets with the sewn-in hoodie are more like Hallmark). It’s the most dramatic garment you can have in your closet, and while wooden top coats are great when it's freezing out, a lighter-weight trench coat works the other nine months of the year—and can be paired with a heavy sweater for the other three. You may not be starring in any blockbusters coming up soon, but, boy, will you look like you're ready to.

In cooler temperatures, a reliable flannel shirt is more than a wardrobe essential: it's a no-brainer. Most versions will be plaid, but all of them should feel substantial enough to double as a light jacket, thanks to their lightweight wool or thick cotton make.

It's hard to think of a jacket more useful, more handsome, more versatile—heck, more all three at once—than the canvas jacket. These days, the original designs still retains their utilitarian charm, but the hammer and nails that used to accompany them have long since been replaced by a cell phone and ear buds. And thanks to fashion's ongoing workwear fixation, there's never been a wider range of luxe designer versions available.

Black derbies can pull through when you need shoes for more formal occasions—and also elevate a quick-and-dirty jeans-and-tee outfit. Dr. Martens are a great entry-level choice, and you'll get a lot more mileage out of the Mono pair, which forgoes the brand's signature yellow stitching for discreet black thread.

When your dress pants are this good—roomy and comfortable, statement-making but versatile—there's no sense in saving them for special occasions. Wear them all the time, with anything, the way you would your jeans.

Belts are often an afterthought, but they really shouldn't be. So don't waist (sorry) the opportunity. Much like cowboy boots, the western belt is riding high in fashion right now—but for this story's purposes, we'd like to guide you back to more classic styles, even if the two belts up top have a certain western flair.

By now, you're probably getting the idea that the name of the game here is versatility. While you could opt for Chelsea boots—the right pair will be able to withstand the elements, and any sideways glances from your office nemesis—you'll feel so much calmer in a pair truly designed to stomping through snowy slush.

We love that iconic North Face puffer as much as the next guy (you know the one we're talking about). But don't let its objectively perfect design distract you from the avalanche of stellar, lesser-known alternatives on the market.

A good duffel bag needs to do only one thing: hold stuff. A great duffel bag, though, needs to check off a few more boxes. It should still carry your clothes, kicks, chargers, toiletries, and everything else in the most space-efficient, easy-to-find way possible. But it should also be designed to outlast your passport—or better yet, you—despite years of being stuffed in an overhead bin and thrown in the trunk of your car. We've tested hundreds of 'em over the years, and the ones below offer all that and more.

#6632. Cranberry Hugo Spritz

A classic Hugo spritz is decidedly a summer cocktail, but if you’re looking for an excuse to pop a bottle of Prosecco in colder weather, look no further than this cranberry Hugo spritz. St-Germain is already my favorite liqueur for its ability to add floral sweetness to a cocktail without being too cloying or overwhelming, but this upgrade to the original Italian spritz gives the elderflower notes additional tartness to play with, creating the perfectly balanced drink for all of your fall and winter parties.

Batch it:Including instructions to make a big batch felt like a no-brainer to make this the easily shareable Friendsgiving centerpiece cocktail that it deserves to be. Just combine the non-bubbly ingredients (mint, lime juice, St-Germain, and cranberry juice) in a pitcher and let your friends finish their glasses with a Prosecco and club soda topper. Keeping the fizzy stuff separate will ensure everyone’s drink feels fresh and properly carbonated. If you mix the bubbly ingredients too soon, they’ll lose their carbonation over time, resulting in a flat, underwhelming sip for those who want a second serving. Leave out a plate of fresh mint and lime slices to let your guests garnish their glasses.

Pro tip:I used unsweetened cranberry juice to develop this, but if you prefer your drinks to be a little on the sweet side, opt for a cranberry juice cocktail. A cranberry juice cocktail is usually blended with other juices and sweetener to tame some of the tartness.

#6631. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6630. Cult Gaia Resort 2027

It may seem like an unlikely starting point for a collection, but designer Jasmin Larian Hekmat’s new resort assortment for Cult Gaia all began with a moth. No, Hekmat was not drawn to replicating its unique biology or wings through her seasonal silhouettes; rather, she was more so drawn to the concept of what the insect represents, and how she could translate that into her signature getaway-ready clothes. “Unlike butterflies, a moth moves by moonlight and light,” says Hekmat. “And for me, the Cult Gaia woman is someone who has the strength and resilience to follow whatever illuminates her.”

The designer’s collections always possess a sense of the upbeat and joyful, so a vision of illumination was no hard concept to follow. For resort, Hekmat doubled down on her signature dresses, though she also ramped up her more casual, day-to-day separates. Dress-wise, there were tons of plissés—one style polka-dotted and cut out at the waist, another in deep emerald with a plunging neckline and high slit. There were more covered-up options, including plenty of lace and crochet gowns, too, in punchy red or minimal whites.

It was interesting to see Hekmat put her twist on everyday staples—infusing basics with that same sense of wanderlust. Her Micah top, for one, had a built-in wavy seams along the front that made a tank seem just a tad more groovy. Or her Tavia sweater imbued with cocoon-like sleeves, drawing right back to her moth inspiration. “You’ll see a lot of pleating techniques that mimic that—I just think nature is so magical,” says Hekmat.

Recently, Hekmat has also been focused on ramping up her menswear offering, and the Cult Gaia man had plenty to play with too. A billowy, PJ-like top and trousers set was finished in sunshine-hued stripes, while a textural black double-breasted suit was a dressier evening option. The men’s fills a big gap in the market—for dudes who need chic, easy vacation wear—and it would be smart for Hekmat to keep building it.

#6629. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6628. Stuffed Pepper Soup

Stuffed peppers are one of the most versatile comfort foods. Literally—put anything in them, and they’ll taste great. The same goes for our stuffed pepper soup recipe. We take the classic stuffed pepper combination of ground beef, rice, tomatoes, and lots of cheese and turn those hearty flavors into an even more comforting soup that you can cozy up to all year long.

Grab a large pot and add in your favorite extra-virgin olive oil. Heat over medium heat, then add in your bell peppers and onion. Cook those down until soft while mixing occasionally—this should take around 7 minutes. Then, you can add the garlic and cook until fragrant, which should only take around 1 minute. Once everything is cooked down and fragrant, add the ground beef and season with salt and pepper. Season generously, but remember that you can always add more later; you can’t take it away. Once the beef is no longer pink, drain the fat and return the pot to the heat.

Once back on the heat, add the broth, crushed tomatoes, diced tomatoes, and your dried oregano. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer. Now it’s time to cook the rice. Add the rice and simmer while covered until the rice is tender. This should take around 40 minutes, but make sure to check on the rice every now and then. If you need a bit more liquid, add a little bit more water. Give it a taste, then season with salt and pepper as needed.

Once your soup is seasoned to your liking, garnish with shredded white cheddar (my personal favorite, but you do you) and some freshly chopped parsley for freshness.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Want to switch up this soup? Start by thinking about your favorite type of stuffed pepper. Do you like yours with ground turkey, ground pork, or sausage? What about using tomato paste for a richer flavor? Tomatillo sauce could replace tomato sauce. White beans, black beans, or navy beans might be the starchy addition if you prefer that over rice. If you’re vegan or vegetarian, fill your soup with zucchini, mushrooms, kale, or other favorite vegetables.

Stuffed pepper soup will last for no more than 3 to 4 days in the fridge. Make sure to seal tightly in a container if there are leftovers or you're meal prepping. The soup will last up to a month in the freezer. Let the soup thaw in the fridge before slowly reheating.

#6627. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.

#6624. 8 Delicious Host Gifts That Aren’t Wine

“What should I bring?” When a guest asks this well-intentioned question, the knee-jerk answer is “Wine!” But it’s just as simple to source thoughtful bits and bobs to create a memorable start to the meal. This way the host can forget about hors d’oeuvres altogether. Pick up a bark-wrapped cheese, artfully marbled charcuterie, or some I-can’t-believe-it’s-store-bought spritzes—or better yet, all of the above—and your fellow diners will be asking where they can buy a box on the way home.

If you are looking to contribute an NA option to the bar, you can’t do better than Ghia’s most recent release, Le Spritz Blood Orange. It’s a bubbly mix of bitter and sweet that more than fills in for an Aperol spritz or predinner glass of prosecco.

The problem with baked Brie is you have to bake it. Instead, bring a soft-rind cheese that can hold its own weight. Set it out on a plate or board for up to an hour before serving; this variety is best eaten at room temp when it’s soft and spreadable and the flavors have bloomed. St. Stephen from Four Fat Fowl in upstate New York is a triple-cream so buttery that even kids will go for seconds. Rush Creek Reserve is a dippable fondue-like wheel wrapped in spruce bark from Uplands in Dodgeville, WI.

The phrase “melts in your mouth” may be oft used and infrequently true, yet the ultramarbled Paleta from Campo Grande actually does. The thinly sliced Ibérico pork shoulder, aged for three years, is Hall of Fame charcuterie board fare. After you set it on the coffee table, don’t walk away, because it’ll be gone by the time you get back.

It’s never been easier to bring quality, ethically sourced caviar to the party. There are lots of sites that will send fish eggs to your door starting around $100. One of our favorites comes from the folks at Island Creek Oysters in Duxbury, MA. They hand-pack their Italian White Sturgeon Caviar and offer next-day shipping. Set out your tin with a thick potato chip (we like Graza or North Fork) and something dairy-rich and creamy (might we recommend labneh?) to balance the brine.

A toasted baguette on bottom, Fishwife’s Cantabrian Anchovies on top, two ways to complete the tartine: Spread a fun cultured butter (we like Frentel, often available at Whole Foods) and you have a classic pintxo. Or, double up on tinned ingredients by adding a layer of Row 7 Sweet Prince Tomatoes and you get a gussied-up pan con tomate.

Find even more thoughtful, creative host gifts this way.

#6622. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.
